On the Minkowski-difference polytope, where the objective is $1$-strongly convex, we prove global linear convergence with explicit constants and no combinatorial swap-step bounds; the per-step contraction is $k$-independent and only the drop-count bound grows with $k$, so aggregation is provably safe while the saving in scans is measured, not proved. Since the TA certificate is the Frank--Wolfe gap divided by the current distance, gap-safe screening applies, and we bound the iteration after which it has removed every zero-weight point off the optimal faces by $O\!\left(\tfrac{k}{\rho}\log\tfrac{1}{\tau}\right)$ up to logarithmic factors in the geometry, $\rho$ the rate constant and $\tau$ the optimal-face margin. On five LIBSVM benchmarks, with fairer baselines than our submission, the solver matches the baselines to four or five digits wherever both converge, ties LIBSVM on sparse-support hard margins and beats our blended pairwise conditional gradients (BPCG). But our full-cache sequential minimal optimisation (SMO) code ties or beats it on kernel $L_2$ margins, LIBLINEAR's dual solver is up to $4.5\times$ faster on the separable $L_2$ margin, and our solver is one to three orders of magnitude slower than LIBLINEAR's Newton solver on dense-support $L_2$ margins and than LIBSVM on a nearly touching kernel hull. Its edge is the certificate, not speed.
  </details>

- **[Testing Central Structure for Complex Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15659)**  `arXiv:2610.15659`  `cs.LG`  
  _Qilong Wu, Yuxiao Li, Simeng Zhang, Xinying Liu, Yan Liu, Zengyou He_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Centrality measures rank nodes even when the observed differences can be explained by ordinary structural variation. We therefore study a preceding question: whether a network contains a statistically identifiable central structure at all. We formulate this question as a network-level hypothesis testing issue using the adjacency spectral radius as the test statistic and estimate an empirical p-value from randomized networks generated under a specified null model. The framework is evaluated using G(N,M), Chung-Lu, and two implementations of the configuration model on simulated benchmarks and 55 real networks. Controlled experiments further vary the number and connection weights of designated central nodes while holding network size and density fixed. The results show a clear negative association between central-structure strength and the empirical p-value. They also demonstrate that rejection decisions depend substantially on the structural properties preserved by the null model: the detected network sets are not simply nested across models.
  </details>

- **[Context-Aware Precision Scheduling for Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15640)**  `arXiv:2610.15640`  `cs.LG`  
  _Mukund Athmaram, Manoj Rao, Liang Ma_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Small language models (SLMs) used as on-device agents must balance accuracy and latency as their context grows. Mixed precision helps manage this tradeoff by assigning different precisions to weight tensors according to their size and sensitivity. However, these choices depend on the operating conditions, so a configuration selected for a short context may no longer provide the best tradeoff at a longer one. We calibrate a timing model from measurements at different precisions and context lengths, and combine it with tensor sensitivities to choose configurations under a latency or accuracy budget. We argue that fewer bits do not always mean faster execution, so our predictor estimates latency from calibrated execution costs rather than weight bytes alone. Under a latency budget, reading the larger key-value (KV) cache leaves less time for weight operations, leading the allocator to select lower precisions. This gives a schedule of tensor changes that can be prepared before execution. Our runtime follows the schedule while retaining the session's KV cache. We evaluate executed schedules on a laptop GPU, including a longer-context schedule with three weight formats and a tool-use benchmark measuring full response time and correctness. Under an accuracy budget, measured error from a quantized KV cache determines the budget left for weights. The allocator can raise or lower weight precision as this estimate changes. These experiments show where context-aware precision helps and where accuracy recovery remains limited.
  </details>

- **[MERIT: Scaling KG Foundation Models with Relation Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15638)**  `arXiv:2610.15638`  `cs.LG`  
  _Cosimo Gregucci, Daniel Hernandez, Antonio Vergari, Steffen Staab_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Knowledge graph (KG) foundation models (KGFMs) predict links on unseen graphs zero-shot. KGFMs have been pioneered by ULTRA which builds a relation graph from co-occurrences that match motif templates, and passes messages over it to obtain relation representations. More recent KGFMs such as MOTIF and TRIX increase the size of this relation graph, and FLOCK replaces message-passing with probabilistic random-walk ensembles. However, larger relation graphs mean more messages, and more walks mean more sequences to encode, so they improve performance at higher training and inference cost. This cost hinders their use in more complex reasoning tasks, such as complex query answering. To reverse this trend, we design MERIT, the first KGFM with a transformer relation encoder: every relation name attends to every other, and the motifs enter as a soft prior rather than as edges. Over 56 benchmarks, MERIT matches the zero-shot MRR of SoTA KGFMs while being 6x faster than TRIX and over 100x faster than FLOCK at inference. Fine-tuned for complex query answering like UltraQuery, MERITQuery improves over it at matched cost.
  </details>

- **[ProML: Progressive Multi-label Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15614)**  `arXiv:2610.15614`  `cs.LG`  
  _Yi Kou, Jieting Wang, Yuhua Qian_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-label learning typically pursues model construction through the joint optimization of label fitting, correlation modeling, and structural regularization. While empirically effective, such a coupled paradigm imposes multiple learning objectives on a single predictive parameter matrix, forcing it to simultaneously fit observed labels and encode structural priors. This coupling may induce ill-conditioned optimization geometry, increase hyper-parameter sensitivity, and complicate capacity control. To address the these issues, this paper proposes a Progressive Multi-Label Learning (ProML) framework, which decouples direct label fitting from predictor learning via the introduction of an auxiliary predictive variable. This auxiliary variable admits a closed-form solution, yielding an equivalent profiled objective in which the supervised fitting term is scaled by a trade-off parameter. This result provides a unified view of ProML and conventional coupled learning, with the latter recovered as a limiting case. We theoretically analyze the optimization geometry of ProML and show that, under quadratic positive semidefinite structural regularization, ProML attenuates the dominant curvature of the fitting term, enlarges the stable learning rate range, and provides a controllable fidelity-regularization trade-off. Further, we instantiate the ProML for multi-label feature selection task by integrating global-local label priors and row-sparse regularization. Extensive experiments and controlled optimization analyses on 12 benchmark datasets empirically corroborate the theoretical analysis and demonstrate the robust and competitive performance of the proposed method.
  </details>

- **[GA-SVD: Generation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for LLM Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15398)**  `arXiv:2610.15398`  `cs.LG`  
  _Shengkun Tang, Cong Zeng, Zongfang Liu, Dan Alistarh, Zhiqiang Shen_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong generalization across a broad range of reasoning and generation tasks, but their large parameter counts impose substantial memory and computation costs, hindering deployment in practical resource-constrained settings. One-shot low-rank compression is a promising solution since it reduces model size and inference cost effectively. However, existing SVD-based methods primarily target multiple-choice benchmarks and often fail to preserve performance on generation tasks. Moreover, their rank allocation strategies are typically heuristic. We propose GA-SVD, a generation-aware low-rank compression framework for LLMs. First, we introduce Generation-Aware Weight Whitening (GAWW), which leverages gradients from on-policy knowledge distillation to construct whitening transformations aligned with generative behavior. Second, we develop an evolutionary global rank allocation method that searches for effective layer-wise rank allocation under a given global compression ratio. Across extensive experiments on Mistral-7B, Qwen3 series, and Llama-3.3 models, evaluated on both multiple-choice and generative benchmarks, GA-SVD consistently outperforms existing SVD-based baselines and achieves state-of-the-art (SoTA) results. We further demonstrate scalability by applying our method to models with up to 70B parameters.
  </details>

- **[WUSPruner: Second-Moment-Optimal Transforms for Structured Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15394)**  `arXiv:2610.15394`  `cs.LG`  
  _Shengkun Tang, Dan Alistarh, Zhiqiang Shen_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Structured pruning is typically formulated as identifying which model dimensions to remove, often within the model's original representation. However, the effect of coordinate deletion fundamentally depends on the basis in which pruning is performed. This raises a more fundamental question: how should the basis be chosen specifically for coordinate deletion? We introduce WUSPruner, a transform-based framework for structured pruning of large language models. We formulate basis selection as a local linear reconstruction problem that directly minimizes the reconstruction loss induced by pruning. Inspired by the second-moment transformation in WUSH, we consider a WUS transform constructed jointly from activation and weight statistics. We show that under positive-definite second moments, WUS transform minimizes the local reconstruction loss over all invertible changes of basis. In the resulting basis, the activation and weight second moments are simultaneously diagonalized and balanced, causing the deletion error to decompose into independent spectral contributions and yielding a principled criterion for coordinate selection. Guided by this result, we develop a scalable pruning method based on blockwise WUS transformations and compact input projections. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models from 8B to 72B parameters show consistent improvements over structured pruning baselines across language modeling, knowledge, commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code generation benchmarks, while also delivering practical reductions in inference latency and memory usage.
  </details>

- **[ANTE: Anticipate, Then Execute -- Learning Internal World Models for Coding Agents from Verified Beliefs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15368)**  `arXiv:2610.15368`  `cs.LG`  
  _Yi Ge, Kangrui Ruan, Jifan Chen, Manish Prajapat, Christian Bock, Xiaoyang Wang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Rapid advances in large language models have made software engineering agents capable of tackling complex coding tasks. Within a containerized environment, a coding agent receives tool responses or execution results, and determines its later actions by those earlier results. However, most existing coding agents never look ahead: their policies do not anticipate the consequences of actions, and the terminal reward barely attributes a failure to certain earlier steps, so an ill-judged edit can corrupt the repository state irreversibly before any signal arrives. Recent code world models aim to address these challenges, but they are either trained and then frozen before reinforcement learning (RL), or reduced to an auxiliary next-token loss on the environment's outputs. We present ANTE (Anticipate, Then Execute), an agentic RL framework that verifies the policy's pre-action predictions by real execution and turns them into per-step credit for its actions and trust-or-abstain decisions. With an internal belief stated before each action, Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) turns the settled predictions into per-step advantages by anchoring credit on the policy's own forecasts. To turn the trained forecasts into better actions at inference, thereby facilitating effective test-time scaling, ANTE-TTO (test-time optimization) selects among candidate actions without an external scorer. ANTE raises Qwen3-32B from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, 6.2% above a matched GRPO baseline trained without the belief state; its world model's accuracy climbs from 44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight capability transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains. In summary, we aim to build a code world model that knows what has happened, what holds now, and what the next action will achieve.
  </details>

- **[Correlation-Aware Reconstruction for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15250)**  `arXiv:2610.15250`  `cs.LG`  
  _Md. Johir Raihan, Zahra Zamanzadeh Darban, Yueyang Liu, Flora D. Salim, Levin Kuhlmann, Mahsa Salehi_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reconstruction-based detectors for multivariate time series anomaly detection typically learn a single entangled representation of normal behavior and flag anomalies based on reconstruction error. However, real-world anomalies are not only isolated spikes in a single channel but also disruptions in the relationships between channels, where each sensor individually appears normal, but their joint behavior deviates from the norm. Because these models compress both temporal evolution and inter-channel structure into this single space, they lack an explicit mechanism to isolate such inter-channel dependencies from normal temporal dependencies, leading to lower detection rates for cross-channel anomalies. We propose CARMA (Correlation-Aware Reconstruction for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection), which is a reconstruction-based variational autoencoder with two complementary latent spaces: a temporal latent that captures sequential dynamics, and a correlation latent that is trained to reconstruct the window's pairwise Pearson correlations. Both representations are fused in the signal decoder, and anomalies are detected from the reconstruction error. We evaluate CARMA on the TSB-AD-M benchmark suite (17 datasets, 180 series) against 29 baseline methods, and show that it significantly outperforms all of them across multiple threshold-free and range-aware metrics, achieving a VUS-PR of 0.4929. Ablations show that removing the correlation branch degrades performance, that adding a second latent without supervision recovers only part of the gain, and that supervising the correlation latent with an explicit correlation target accounts for the rest and produces a sharper error response at anomalies.
  </details>

- **[Anchors Enhance Controllability and Reasoning of Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15097)**  `arXiv:2610.15097`  `cs.LG`  
  _Feiyu Qu, Zheng Huang, Andrea Zanette_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer new opportunities for controllable text generation. However, their controllability, defined as the ability to satisfy task constraints while preserving their original capabilities, remains underexplored. DLMs' bidirectional attention allows control tokens to guide generation from arbitrary positions in the output sequence, but effective guidance depends on the compatibility between their content and placement. To this end, we propose AnchorDLM, a framework in which an anchor generator produces an anchor consisting of a short output fragment and its position for each query. The anchor is placed as control tokens at the specified position to initialize the output sequence of a frozen DLM and guide subsequent denoising. We train the anchor generator with reinforcement learning (RL) to jointly optimize anchor content and placement, using rewards computed from the DLM's generated outputs based on answer correctness and constraint satisfaction. Moreover, through the lens of discrete flow matching (DFM), we interpret anchor placement as helping to reshape the initial velocity field that guides generation. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning across five DLM backbones show that AnchorDLM improves controllability and further yields gains in reasoning performance across diverse benchmarks.
  </details>

- **[Swarm Telepathy: Prefill-Free KV-Cache Transfer Across Families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15095)**  `arXiv:2610.15095`  `cs.LG`  
  _Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Irene Tenison, Yang Zhang, Yada Zhu, Boris Katz, Dan Gutfreund_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM multi-agent systems split work across agents that communicate through text. An agent summarizes its findings, another agent receives the text. This constrains communication to discrete tokens and costs redundant compute, limiting bandwidth and capabilities of multi-agent systems. Recent works demonstrate KV-cache transfer between LLMs but they either require the LLMs to be within the same family or cannot function across context, thus requiring the receiver to prefill text. We present SwaT (Swarm Telepathy), the first cross-family KV-cache transfer method that allows prefill-free communication in multi-family multi-agent systems. In an agent-to-agent communication setting, combining SwaT with recent advances in KV-cache compaction beats text-to-text communication in both accuracy and speed, with a mean of $40\%$ higher accuracy and a mean of $4\times$ faster wall-clock time. Experiments show SwaT achieves high performance on 17 benchmarks across 12 LLMs and 6 families. Additionally, given a sender Vision-Language Model (VLM), SwaT is able to transfer the vision capabilities to a text-only receiver LLM exceeding text-to-text communication despite SwaT being trained on text-only data. SwaT keeps both sender and receiver models frozen without fine-tuning and only requires $<50M$ tokens and $<1$ GPU-day to train.
  </details>

- **[The Optimal Decoder is Tilted Temperature](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15058)**  `arXiv:2610.15058`  `cs.LG`  
  _Nikolaos Papagiannis, Ananth Grama, Wojciech Szpankowski_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Larger sample budgets benefit from higher sampling temperatures in LLMs, but what temperature tuning optimizes and why it works remain poorly understood. We seek to answer these questions: we pose decoding as pass@$k$ maximization subject to two constraints that encode critical decoding failure modes: an entropy floor preventing diversity collapse, and a cross-entropy ceiling preventing implausibility. We prove that this maximization takes the form of a single closed-form conditional sampling rule, the \emph{tilted temperature} $q^\star \propto \bigl(p e^{\eta V}\bigr)^{1/T}$. Here, the tilt comes from a verifier potential $V$ that quantifies how likely a partial generation is to eventually pass. Ordinary temperature sampling, verifier-greedy decoding, and reward-tilted policies represent special cases. We further show that, under a natural rule for scaling the diversity budget with sample size $k$, the resulting optimal temperature increases with $k$, turning empirical choice into a theorem. The optimum still needs the unknown verifier potential, which we estimate using two design approaches. In the online setting, our J-EOS algorithm jointly tracks the two constraint multipliers and learns the verifier potential from binary pass/ fail feedback alone. In the offline setting, we show that when the model is calibrated, its log-probability tracks correctness up to an affine map. Under this condition, the tilt collapses into the exponent and the optimum reduces to ordinary temperature sampling. Calibrated Temperature Decoding (CTD) then fits one scalar offline and samples with zero additional inference-time overhead relative to temperature sampling. Building on these decision rules, we design a practical decoding algorithm for code generation and evaluate it alongside CTD on benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP, showing improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines.
  </details>

- **[PATTERN Can Be Solved from Memory: Generator-Aware Baselines for Synthetic Node Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15020)**  `arXiv:2610.15020`  `cs.LG`  
  _Amin Najafgholizadeh, Mohsen Afsharchi_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  PATTERN, a synthetic node-classification benchmark still used to rank graph networks, plants a random subgraph in a random host graph and asks which nodes belong to it. Its generator draws 100 patterns once and plants the same ones in every split, so each test graph carries a pattern that also appears in 100 training graphs. A matcher that reads these patterns off the training labels and looks them up in each test graph reaches 99.2 class-weighted accuracy with no trained parameters, against 89.8 for the best published model. Inference under the generator without the patterns reaches 86.8. Two published models, CKGConv and GRIT, score lower on patterns they have not seen: on new graphs with fresh patterns both fall below this pattern-blind predictor, and withholding patterns from CKGConv's training lowers its accuracy on the test graphs that carry them. Training CKGConv with a new pattern in every graph raises its accuracy on fresh patterns by about 2 points, to the level of the pattern-blind predictor, at some cost on the reused patterns. The same kind of inference under the generator matches the best published result on CLUSTER and, without any training, scores above every published result we found on Minesweeper's released board. We recommend that synthetic benchmarks report scores on fresh templates beside reused ones, publish baselines built from their generators, and state how their metric is weighted and pooled.
  </details>

- **[Pro-t-VAE: Closed-Form Student's t Mixtures for Robust Prototype Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14894)**  `arXiv:2610.14894`  `cs.LG`  
  _Zhikang Xu, Jiarui Xing, Jian Wang_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present a robust deep generative framework for unsupervised image prototype discovery, built on a heavy-tailed Student's t mixture prior, that bridges statistical robustness and mathematical tractability. Existing generative approaches typically rely on noise-prone Gaussian priors or computationally intensive diffusion models; neither simultaneously provides explicit latent structure nor exact analytic optimization. While diffusion models can yield strong priors, iterative sampling and intractable likelihoods limit scalability and interpretability for prototype discovery. We address these issues by constructing a Student's t latent space via a Bayesian scale-mixture formulation. This yields a fully closed-form augmented ELBO for unsupervised Student's t mixture variational autoencoders, which, to our knowledge, is the first such objective applied to robust image prototype discovery, avoiding biased variational approximations and high computational costs in prior heavy-tailed or diffusion-based frameworks. Treating precision as a latent variable automatically modulates each data point's influence, downweighting outliers to learn a data-dependent measure of trust. The result is improved robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, with well-separated latent representations and more stable manifold learning than state-of-the-art methods. We validate our model on standard vision benchmarks and challenging neuroimaging tasks. In brain MRI-driven neurodegenerative disease analysis, our model recovers clean, anatomically coherent prototypes where clinical noise often collapses rare subtypes. These results highlight the ability of our framework to preserve anatomy-associated patterns for precise discovery in clinical settings. Our code is available at:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[Contrastive Linearized Laplace: Loss Geometry, Valid Repairs, and Reliable Cores](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14875)**  `arXiv:2610.14875`  `cs.LG`  
  _Francisco J. Sáez-Maldonado, Luis A. Ortega, Andrés R. Masegosa, Thomas D. Nielsen_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While contrastive learning is widely used to learn deterministic representations, it does not inherently provide estimates of uncertainty. Post-hoc uncertainty estimation methods, such as the Linearized Laplace approximation (LLA), offer a way to quantify uncertainty without retraining the encoder. However, we show that directly using the LLA induced distribution over the contrastive embedding does not yield reliable pointwise uncertainty estimates for downstream tasks: embedding variance alone does not reflect whether decisions such as nearest-neighbor retrieval or cluster assignment are stable. To address this limitation, we develop a post-hoc framework based on LLA that propagates encoder uncertainty through the downstream task. We characterize the curvature of contrastive objectives and introduce positive-semidefinite repairs where needed to obtain valid local Gaussian approximations without retraining the encoder. We test the proposed approach in metagenomic binning and image classification tasks. For metagenomic binning, posterior coassignment probabilities support consensus partitions and the selection of reliable cores, leading to improvements over existing baselines. Additional image classification experiments show calibration improvements on standard benchmarks and real histopathology datasets.
  </details>

- **[World2TS: Real-World Event Context for Time-Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14861)**  `arXiv:2610.14861`  `cs.LG`  
  _Zhiding Liu, Jiqian Yang, Mingyue Cheng, Zhi Li, Enhong Chen_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Time-series forecasting plays a vital role in a wide range of real-world applications. Recent approaches have achieved strong performance by modeling temporal correlations and cross-channel dependencies, yet most forecasting benchmarks still represent time series primarily as numerical histories. In practice, time series are observations of complex real-world processes, and their trajectories may reflect events, interventions, disruptions, and changes in measurement or reporting that cannot always be inferred from past values alone. A central barrier to studying context-aware forecasting is therefore the lack of large-scale datasets that align real-world events with the individual series they affect. We present World2TS, a scalable construction framework and large-scale dataset for time-series forecasting with real-world event context. We first develop world2ts-core, a reusable tool that combines agent-led semantic reasoning and Web search, command-line execution and validation, and human review within a feedback-driven discovery workflow. Given heterogeneous time series with semantic descriptions, the workflow discovers candidate events, consolidates retrieved evidence into verified events, and links them to relevant series under explicit temporal and semantic scopes. Using this framework, we construct world2ts-data, which contains 31 datasets across six domains, comprising 4,179 series, 97.1 million observations, 1,159 events, and 56,846 event-series links. We further conduct extensive data analyses and controlled comparative experiments to characterize the dataset and demonstrate the utility of the collected context for improving forecasting accuracy. World2TS provides a reusable data foundation for developing and evaluating context-aware forecasting models and agents. The project homepage is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Terrarium: Growing Personal Assistants via Scalable Synthesis of App Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14860)**  `arXiv:2610.14860`  `cs.LG`  
  _Mengzhou Wu, Yuzhe Guo, Jiawen Tao, Xiaokun Yuan, Yuan Cao, Gang Cao, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought the vision of a general-purpose personal assistant closer to reality. Such assistants could provide a unified natural-language interface to a broad ecosystem of applications. However, real-world applications do not readily support training at scale because access is often restricted and their state is difficult to reset. To address this challenge, we introduce Terrarium, a framework that synthesizes executable App Worlds from real-world application information, generates training task packages with evaluator-side rubrics from these worlds, and iteratively validates and refines both through agent rollouts. For App World synthesis, Terrarium organizes public Web information and in-application observations into structured app specifications that guide the construction of self-contained runtimes with callable operations and mutable, resettable state. For task synthesis, Terrarium constructs tasks grounded in App World state together with evaluator-side outcome rubrics that assess success without prescribing reference trajectories. We construct a training suite of 275 App Worlds and 13,344 tasks for outcome-based reinforcement learning across three Qwen3 model scales (4B, 8B, and 14B parameters). Across these scales, models trained with Terrarium outperform the corresponding Qwen3 models by an average of 18.34 percentage points on the $\tau^2$-bench and 10.94 percentage points on the AppWorld bench. These results suggest that app-grounded world and task synthesis offers a scalable path toward general-purpose assistants capable of operating across broad application ecosystems.
  </details>

- **[Sequence-Structured Decision Learning for Branch-and-Bound in Mixed-Integer Linear Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14835)**  `arXiv:2610.14835`  `cs.LG`  
  _Tengfei Liu, Jinrun Liu, Bai Yan, Yuhui Shi, Qi Zhao_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Branch-and-bound (BnB) solves mixed-integer linear programs by constructing and exploring a search tree. Node selection and branching are two recurrent decisions that directly determine the tree. Learning-based approaches typically optimize either decision in isolation and condition on a mostly local view, leaving the coupled evolution of the search tree insufficiently modeled. This paper proposes Seq-BnB, a sequence-structured framework that learns branching and node selection from a shared global representation of the evolving BnB process. Seq-BnB serializes node creations, node updates, node-selection events, and branching events into typed tokens, producing a causal event sequence of the search trajectory. A self-attention encoder summarizes this global search history, a bipartite graph neural network encodes the current LP relaxation, and context-conditioned decision heads score branching variables and open nodes. To reduce distribution shift between expert demonstrations and learned policies, Seq-BnB is trained with DAgger-style data aggregation. On four MILP benchmark families, Seq-BnB consistently processes fewer BnB nodes than heuristic and learning-based baselines, with strong solution times on both standard and larger transfer instances. While this paper evaluates Seq-BnB instantiation for branching and node selection, it accommodates additional solver decisions, such as cut selection, by introducing new action tokens and decision heads.
  </details>

- **[Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Dengue Infection Using Clinical and Hematological Data from Bangladesh: A Comparative Analysis of Benchmark and Extended Prediction Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14813)**  `arXiv:2610.14813`  `cs.LG`  
  _Neesha Naimeen, Victor Miranda Soberanis_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Dengue is a viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV) and a major public health concern in Bangladesh, where symptom overlap with other febrile illnesses complicates early diagnosis. This study compares Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost to predict dengue from clinical and hematological data using two Bangladeshi hospital datasets (2024, n=1,511; 2025, n=1,283) with SMOTE. Extended models outperformed benchmarks within 2024 (Random Forest ROC-AUC 0.640 to 0.661), with RDW-CV the most consistently influential added predictor. 2025 benchmark performance was higher (ROC-AUC 0.904), unexplained by class imbalance and possibly reflecting data quality. External validation is needed.
  </details>

- **[CrossMean: Model Merging by Pairing Merged and Expert Activations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14762)**  `arXiv:2610.14762`  `cs.LG`  
  _Moshe Eliasof_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Model merging combines fine-tuned experts into one network without retraining, and closed-form methods compute each merged layer from statistics of its input activations. However, these statistics are measured on a single expert, while in the merged model, each layer receives activations from the merged layers that precede it. Recent work re-measures these statistics in the merged model but still forms them from a single network. We formulate closed-form methods as a linear system and show that they use the same matrix on both sides. We then introduce CrossMean, which replaces this matrix on one side with a bilinear statistic that pairs merged and expert activations. From the same statistics, we also derive a label-free criterion that indicates the task sets in which accounting for the merged activations improves the merge more. Empirically, task sets with a lower criterion value show a larger improvement. On the eight-task benchmark of each vision backbone that we tested and on BERT encoders, CrossMean improves on merging with statistics measured on the experts, and with all linear layers merged, it also improves on re-measuring these statistics in the merged model. These results suggest that merging benefits from pairing merged and expert activations.
  </details>

- **[VitaBench: Memory Lifecycles Beyond Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14731)**  `arXiv:2610.14731`  `cs.LG`  
  _Muquan Yu, Dihan Hu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long-term memory benchmarks for language agents primarily evaluate whether information from earlier interactions can be retrieved and used when relevant. Persistent memory systems face an additional problem before future use is known: deciding whether a memory should remain exact, be compressed, consolidated, or deleted. Existing benchmarks capture long-range retrieval, temporal reasoning, evidence reuse, and incremental interaction, but do not directly evaluate these earlier representation decisions. We formalize memory lifecycle evaluation and introduce VitaBench, a benchmark that makes lifecycle decisions measurable through repeated memory reviews and full-horizon counterfactual evaluation. VitaBench contains a controlled Diagnostic tier that isolates future-use patterns and a Naturalistic tier that composes them into generated customer-service-style interaction streams. We characterize lifecycle decision structure with three diagnostics: lifecycle headroom, measuring the advantage of adaptive choices over the best fixed strategy; horizon reversal, measuring when short-horizon decisions change under delayed consequences; and optimal-action diversity, measuring whether different memory states favor different lifecycle operations. Across both tiers, VitaBench exhibits substantial lifecycle structure: lifecycle headroom is 1.364 in Diagnostic and 1.405 in Naturalistic, and 60.2% and 56.5% of states, respectively, change their preferred action between short and full horizons. A learned delayed lifecycle policy further improves over the best fixed strategy on VitaBench-Naturalistic, reaching 101.5 versus 83.4 joint utility. These results show that retrieving past information and deciding how it should persist are distinct evaluation problems, and that lifecycle management requires evaluation of the delayed consequences of representation decisions.
  </details>

- **[DeKoR: Decomposed Knowledge Routing for Efficient GNN--LLM Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14710)**  `arXiv:2610.14710`  `cs.LG`  
  _Peiyuan Li, Yongqi Huang, Jitao Zhao, Di Jin, Dongxiao He_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for text-attributed graph learning by leveraging rich pre-trained knowledge and language understanding capabilities. Combining LLMs with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offers a promising paradigm for expanding the modeling capabilities of graph learning. However, LLMs and GNNs follow distinct learning paradigms, leading to a pronounced mismatch between their knowledge spaces. Such discrepancies make effective knowledge fusion nontrivial. Moreover, existing methods often incur substantial additional computation for only limited performance gains. To address these challenges, we propose DeKoR, an efficient framework for GNN and LLM knowledge fusion. To enable efficient knowledge transfer, DeKoR decomposes LLM knowledge into complementary local and global views and uses the LLM as an offline teacher to distill them into lightweight experts. To enable selective knowledge fusion, an adaptive router learns how much each node should rely on each expert. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that DeKoR outperforms existing baselines on both node and subgraph classification, achieving superior effectiveness and efficiency.
  </details>

- **[From Rainfall to Road-Network Functionality: Transferable Graph Forecasting for Flood-Disrupted Transportation Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14622)**  `arXiv:2610.14622`  `cs.LG`  
  _Junyan Wang, Naiyu Wang_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Extreme rainfall can rapidly degrade road-network functionality (RNF), disrupting emergency mobility, accessibility, evacuation, logistics, and infrastructure restoration. Existing flood-transportation impact models are often difficult to deploy across regions because they rely on local calibration, intensive simulation workflows or target-region retraining. This study proposes G-R2R, a transferable spatiotemporal graph-learning framework that reframes rainfall-induced road-network disruption as a region-conditioned, topology-flexible graph forecasting problem for unseen transportation networks. The framework integrates ego-centered subgraph sampling, terrain-conditioned graph representation, region-conditioned dual-level static encoding, and dynamic rainfall-network feature learning. Static geographic and infrastructure attributes are fused with rainfall forcing and recent RNF states to forecast node-level RNF across heterogeneous road networks. G-R2R is evaluated using simulation-derived RNF sequences from ten flood-prone regions in Wenzhou, China, under unseen-region testing protocols. It outperforms representative forecasting baselines, achieving a stabilized MAPE of 2.33% and $R^2$ of 0.855 under the fixed unseen-region benchmark. Leave-one-area-out evaluation yields stabilized MAPE values of 2.30%-3.54%. Ablation analysis supports the contributions of the terrain-conditioned graph representation and dual-level static encoding. A historical-event replay of Typhoon Fitow further shows that G-R2R reproduces principal temporal trajectories and node-level spatial patterns of the simulation-derived RNF reference under observed rainfall forcing without target-region retraining. These results support rapid and transferable node-level RNF forecasting across the regional road-network domains represented in this study.
  </details>

- **[PGSB: Pretrained-Guided Shared Basis for LoRA Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14558)**  `arXiv:2610.14558`  `cs.LG`  
  _Muqing Liu, Chongjie Si, Zhuoya Liu, Yuheng Jia_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large pretrained models have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, yet adapting them to multiple downstream tasks remains challenging: full fine-tuning is costly, while maintaining separate task-specific models is storage-inefficient and fails to produce a unified multi-task model. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) offers an efficient alternative for Model Merging by representing each task adaptation as a low-rank update over frozen pretrained weights. However, existing LoRA merging methods often treat task-specific updates as directly comparable objects and merge them in their original low-rank parameter spaces. This overlooks two key factors: which update directions provide reliable shared support across tasks, and how these directions should be re-parameterized with respect to the pretrained weights before merging. To address this limitation, we propose Pretrained-Guided Shared Basis (PGSB), a two-stage framework for LoRA model merging. PGSB first identifies shared directions among task-specific LoRA updates, and then re-parameterizes these directions using their interaction with the pretrained weights, producing a more suitable basis for merging. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PGSB consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across multiple benchmarks. Codes are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[A Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM) for Physically-Interpretable Rainfall-Evapotranspiration-Runoff Simulation Across Diverse Hydroclimatic Regimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14493)**  `arXiv:2610.14493`  `cs.LG`  
  _M Jawad, HV Gupta, MA Farmani, A Behrangi, GY Niu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent advances in machine learning have improved rainfall-runoff prediction, yet most data-driven models remain difficult to interpret and do not explicitly enforce physical conservation laws. We present the Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM), a mass-conserving architecture based on the Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP). GCHM uses five storage states representing canopy interception, snow, soil moisture, groundwater, and streamflow generation. Constrained gates govern precipitation partitioning, evapotranspiration, infiltration, seepage, runoff, and baseflow while learning context-dependent process relationships.We evaluate GCHM across 50 CAMELS catchments spanning snowmelt-dominated, recent-rainfall, historical-rainfall, and arid regimes, using NOAA AORC meteorological forcing and remotely sensed vegetation and land-surface data. Performance is assessed using the Jawad-Kling-Gupta Efficiency (JKGE) metric, which accounts for stationary and non-stationary hydrologic behavior. We compare the full architecture with ablated variants and recurrent neural network benchmarks.GCHM reproduces streamflow dynamics across diverse hydroclimatic regimes, including arid catchments, while maintaining interpretable states and fluxes. Ablation experiments show that simplified architectures may perform adequately under wet conditions but struggle to represent flow persistence and recession during dry periods, when groundwater storage sustains low flows. Learned gates recover hydrologically plausible relationships governing snowmelt, runoff, seepage, and evapotranspiration. GCHM combines competitive predictive performance with mass conservation and interpretability, providing a foundation for hydrologic modeling and counterfactual analysis.
  </details>

- **[Sparse-TD-JEPA: Improving Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning With Sparse Latent Task Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14400)**  `arXiv:2610.14400`  `cs.LG`  
  _Duaa Nakshbandi, Zhiyu An, Wan Du_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Successor-feature-based zero-shot reinforcement learning methods pre-train a task encoder and successor-feature predictor on offline, reward-free data, then recover a policy at test time by solving a closed-form linear regression over a small labeled dataset. We identify an underexplored limitation of this approach: when the task encoder produces dense representations, the inferred reward signal becomes diffuse across the state space, reducing the contrast between goal-relevant states and the background and providing a weaker signal for the policy to follow. We address this limitation by introducing an l1 sparsity penalty that concentrates reward-predictive structure into a smaller effective subspace of the task encoder's latent space. The penalty is applied only during training and requires no architectural change or modification to the closed-form inference procedure. We instantiate this approach as Sparse-TD-JEPA, a single-line of code addition based on Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (TD-JEPA) that significantly improved its performance in zero-shot reinforcement learning. We evaluate Sparse-TD-JEPA on 65 tasks across the DeepMind Control (DMC) Suite and OGBench, covering locomotion, navigation, trajectory stitching, puzzle solving, and robotic manipulation. Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons. On DMC, it increases the average return from 661 +- 6 to 714 +- 3. On OGBench, it increases the average success rate from 38.0 +- 0.8 to 48.4 +- 2.3, with improvements of 13.4-18.0 percentage points on the evaluated antmaze navigation and stitching domains. Overall, Sparse-TD-JEPA achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in nine of the 13 domains. Analysis further shows that sparsity produces a sharper and more task-informative inferred reward landscape.
  </details>

- **[Historical Anchors for Scientific Forecasting on Human-Aware Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14023)**  `arXiv:2610.14023`  `cs.LG`  
  _Siu Tin Wu, Ryan C. Barron, Phoebe Upton Sanderbeck, Kim Ø. Rasmussen, George Tompkins, Maksim E. Eren_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Predicting which scientific connections will form next can point researchers toward the most promising leads. One successful approach learns representations by sampling paths through publication networks, represented by a hypergraph, that connect scientific entities, concepts, and researchers, approximating how knowledge and expertise move through the literature. Sampled paths are then used to train an embedding model to forecast scientific connections such as a property of a material. Performance, however, depends strongly on how many paths are sampled: too little sampling yields incomplete representations, while further sampling can eventually weaken prediction quality. The best sampling budget is therefore often identifiable only after future discoveries are known. We introduce Query--Anchor Agreement (QAA), a diagnostic requiring no future labels or separately trained model. QAA can be used to select a sampling budget, and refine or re-rank the resulting forecast to improve forecasting scientific connections. QAA compares the candidates a model predicts for a target with those most similar to the target's known historical examples, and identifies when these two views converge. Across thermoelectric-material and COVID-19 drug-repurposing benchmarks, repeated random-seed runs, and three sampling policies, QAA-selected budgets fall on average 1.86 percentage points below hindsight-optimal selection for broad candidate recovery. Further, promoting candidates supported by both views, under a capped fusion that bounds the anchor contribution, improves broad recovery across all six benchmark-policy settings, which define the types of network walks used for sampling.
  </details>

- **[LACRM: LLM-Guided Mining of Directed Advertiser Competition Relationships in E-Commerce Advertising](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13959)**  `arXiv:2610.13959`  `cs.LG`  
  _Xiang Shi, Yitian Kou, Bing Li, Shengsheng Niu, Chun Gan, Linghui Meng, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In e-commerce advertising, ad platforms typically fail to model the externalities among advertisers when making optimization decisions: an advertiser's actual performance is largely shaped by rivals competing for the same users; these rivals typically operate in overlapping product categories and at comparable budget scales. However, capturing this rivalry as an explicit, reusable signal is challenging because it is directed, multi-faceted, and partially observable. Existing paradigms such as interaction graphs, taxonomy rules, and single-embedding models do not fully capture these properties. In this paper, we propose LACRM (LLM-driven Advertiser Competition Relationship Mining), a novel framework that constructs directed competition graphs with continuous edge intensities via a three-stage pipeline. LACRM moves beyond symmetric similarity through LLM-driven role-separated profiling, which enables asymmetric multi-route retrieval to uncover both realized and latent rivals. The framework further incorporates listwise learning-to-rank aligned with temporal auction behavior to accurately model directed competition intensity. In offline retrieval experiments on an industrial benchmark, LACRM outperforms strong directed GNN baselines and ablation variants. Multi-LLM and human studies provide complementary evidence that the recovered latent rivals reflect meaningful market competition rather than merely model-generated artifacts. In production A/B tests, LACRM-guided bidding and incentive allocation increase advertising revenue by 1.73% and 1.14%, respectively. The results demonstrate the practical value of explicit competition modeling in large-scale advertising systems.
  </details>

- **[TabMF: Learning Dataset Representations with Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13818)**  `arXiv:2610.13818`  `cs.LG`  
  _Rafiq Kamel, Nicolas Atienza, Aziz Fouché, Nicola Cancedda, Josif Grabocka_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Representations of supervised datasets support higher-level machine-learning tasks such as dataset retrieval and distribution-shift monitoring. However, existing approaches typically rely either on hand-crafted meta-features or on dataset encoders trained specifically for representation learning. We introduce TabMF, a framework that repurposes pretrained tabular foundation models (TFMs) as encoders of supervised datasets. TabMF equips a predictive TFM with an architecture-aware dataset-level readout and adapts the model end-to-end using contrastive post-training on stochastic views of synthetic supervised datasets. We instantiate TabMF on TabICLv2 and TabPFN-2.5 and evaluate the resulting representations across six tasks on unseen real datasets. Simple frozen TFM readouts yield competitive representations, indicating that predictive pretraining already induces substantial dataset-level structure. The two TabMF encoders obtain the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated learned and classical dataset representations, with particularly strong results in dataset retrieval, compact benchmark construction, and distribution-shift severity assessment.
  </details>

- **[CityDeploy-Bench: Benchmarking Physics-Grounded Spatial Set Planning for Multi-Transmitter Network Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11065)**  `arXiv:2610.11065`  `cs.LG`  
  _Chenyang Yuan, Xiaoyuan Cheng_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Automating city-scale wireless deployment remains challenging under complex urban propagation and network-wide interference. We introduce \textbf{CityDeploy-Bench}, a benchmark that reframes multi-transmitter deployment as \emph{physics-grounded spatial set planning} under a unified ray-tracing verifier. The benchmark separates utility representation from planning dynamics, enabling controlled comparison between direct scalar rewards, relational models, and higher-order interaction structures across diverse planners. Our experiments reveal a clear transition in planning behavior as physical coupling grows. Deployment quality becomes increasingly dependent on whether the learned utility captures collective transmitter interactions, whereas stronger search alone cannot compensate for missing relational structure. This establishes multi-transmitter deployment as a coordination problem over physically interacting sets rather than a collection of independent spatial decisions. We release CityDeploy-Data and the benchmark framework as a reproducible testbed for research linking decision learning with physically grounded wireless network design.
  </details>

- **[QiYao-I: A Manifold Based Foundation Model for Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06936)**  `arXiv:2610.06936`  `cs.LG`  
  _Linfeng Wang, Ruitong Zhang, Kai Zhao, Yang Shu, Zhongwen Rao, Meng Wang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Irregular multivariate time series forecasting is a challenging yet important problem in real-world applications, where observations are often irregularly sampled and asynchronously recorded across variables. Existing time series foundation models are mostly built on regularly sampled sequences, making them difficult to generalize to irregular time intervals and asynchronous cross-variable dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose QiYao-I, a manifold based foundation model for irregular multivariate time series forecasting. Specifically, we introduce a novel sampling-conditioned temporal manifold attention mechanism that maps real timestamps into a learnable temporal manifold feature space and injects temporal manifold biases into attention layers, enabling the model to capture both irregular time intervals and local sampling structures. Further, we propose a dynamic variable interaction mechanism with frequency awareness. It selectively performs cross-variable message passing under asynchronous observations. Extensive experiments on real-world irregular multivariate forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that QiYao-I achieves superior performance compared with both time series foundation models and end-to-end irregular forecasting models, showing strong generalization ability in zero-shot and few-shot settings.
  </details>

- **[Localized Operator Learning with Adaptive Partition-of-Unity Mixture-of-Expert Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04708)**  `arXiv:2610.04708`  `cs.LG`  
  _Madison Cooley, Ramansh Sharma, Shandian Zhe, Robert M. Kirby, Varun Shankar_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Operator learning methods such as DeepONets and FNOs often struggle with PDE families featuring sharp interfaces, heterogeneous coefficients, and localized multiscale structures. We introduce a partition-of-unity (POU) mixture-of-experts framework for localized operator learning, in which geometry-aware gating networks produce smooth spatial partitions which blend the contributions of local expert networks. Our main contribution is HiRefPOU, a residual-style hierarchical POU architecture for DeepONets that organizes localized representations through nested parent-child partitions while preserving global continuity. We also show that the same POU principle can be incorporated into Fourier Neural Operators to introduce spatial adaptivity without modifying the underlying spectral layers. On heterogeneous Darcy and reaction-diffusion benchmarks, HiRefPOU achieves substantially lower error than global DeepONet and static POU-MoE baselines, while the broader operator-learning experiments show that the benefits of localization depend on the PDE structure and the chosen neural-operator backbone. The learned partitions are interpretable and align with interfaces and regions of rapid solution variation. These results show that explicit geometric localization can improve both accuracy and interpretability in neural operator learning.
  </details>

- **[Are We Recovering Mechanisms? Objective-Level Recovery Gaps in Mechanistic Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02098)**  `arXiv:2610.02098`  `cs.LG`  
  _Chuqin Geng, Li Zhang, Haolin Ye, Mark Zhang, Luke Zhang, Xujie Si_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Mechanistic interpretability aims to recover the internal computations responsible for model behavior. Progress in automated circuit discovery is often framed as a search problem: better attribution or optimization should identify better mechanisms. This assumes that the evaluation objective can recognize a better circuit once it is found. Yet standard intervention-based evaluation replaces signals outside a circuit to isolate its effect, changing the computational environment in which the retained components operate. We call this change context distortion. This raises the question of whether faithfulness rewards recovery of model behavior or compatibility with the altered context. We show that intervention-based faithfulness can prefer an equally sized circuit that reproduces the model's behavior less well. We call this reversal misranking, an objective-level recovery gap. To isolate evaluation from discovery, we construct equally sized candidates through controlled edits to human-identified circuits in pretrained language models, including IOI and Greater-Than, and benchmark circuits with known mechanisms. We find misranking even without a discovery algorithm. Misranking also occurs in real automated circuit-discovery settings. Among outputs of EAP, EAP-IG, ACDC, and Edge-SP, KL faithfulness under ordinary resampling prefers the behaviorally worse candidate in 13.2%-24.4% of candidate pairs across these methods on four pretrained-language-model tasks. Finally, restoring selected intact-model signals reverses 96 of 100 selected persistent misrankings, demonstrating that context distortion contributes to these failures. In light of these findings, we call for rethinking both how circuit discovery is performed and how its results are evaluated.
  </details>

- **[Sim+Real: Joint Simulation-Experiment Training Improves Balanced Prediction in Physical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01974)**  `arXiv:2610.01974`  `cs.LG`  
  _Mahindra Rautela, Alexander Scheinker, Ayan Biswas, Diane Oyen, Nathan DeBardeleben, Earl Lawrence_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Simulation and experimental measurements provide complementary data for learning spatiotemporal physical systems, but standard simulation-to-experiment fine-tuning optimizes only the experimental objective after transfer and can degrade simulation performance. We formulate simulation--experiment prediction as a multi-objective learning problem with domain-specific simulation and experimental risks. On four fluid systems from RealPDEBench and two model capacities, we compare Simulation only, Experiment only, Sim$\rightarrow$Exp, and Joint training, evaluating every final model on both held-out domains. Sim$\rightarrow$Exp tends to specialize more strongly to experimental data at the cost of simulation-domain forgetting. Joint training consistently achieves the best balanced performance over a broad range of simulation--experiment evaluation weightings, while substantially improving simulation retention over Sim$\rightarrow$Exp. Joint also better preserves simulation-only fields absent from experimental measurements. Project page:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[TrueMuse: A Benchmark for Data Attribution in Text-to-Music Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00835)**  `arXiv:2610.00835`  `cs.LG`  
  _Jiawei Yu, Jian Liu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Text-to-music generation models are trained on massive music collections, creating a growing need for data attribution methods that can quantify the contribution of individual training samples. However, existing attribution methods are difficult to rigorously evaluate due to the lack of reliable ground truth, making it challenging to reliably assess their actual effectiveness. To address this gap, we introduce TrueMuse, a controlled dataset and benchmark for text-to-music data attribution. TrueMuse is constructed by fine-tuning three diffusion-based text-to-music models on carefully curated attribution samples, whose known inclusion in fine-tuning provides controlled attribution targets for evaluation. The benchmark covers four attribution settings, spanning melodic structure, timbral characteristics, artist-level stylistic signatures, and genre-level shared patterns, and includes 133 attributes, 648 fine-tuned models, and 95,456 generated samples across two prompt types. Using TrueMuse, we systematically evaluate existing black-box attribution methods along four dimensions: fine-tuning improvement, prompt-type difficulty, multi-task training, and fine-tuning data size. Our results show that attribution remains challenging, with existing methods exhibiting substantial variation across evaluation settings, highlighting the need for more reliable and generalizable attribution methods for text-to-music generation.
  </details>

- **[SkillSpec: Consensus-Gated Agent Skill Evolution via Representation Specialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00704)**  `arXiv:2610.00704`  `cs.LG`  
  _Huancheng Chen, Xiaodi Sun, Zhaoqiong Huang, Shenyang Huang, Shreya Singhal, Jingwen Lu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Natural-language skills are textual procedural memories through which large language model (LLM) agents retain reusable task knowledge without updating model weights. Existing methods typically treat skills as either static artifacts or monolithic documents optimized using aggregate validation scores as feedback. However, representing a skill as a monolithic document restricts optimization to its textual content, without explicitly modeling the structure through which procedural knowledge is retrieved and executed. We identify a key distinction between learning what knowledge to retain and determining how to organize it: textual updates should first be validated through execution evidence, after which the retained knowledge should be structured according to its procedural dependencies and retrieval requirements. To this end, we introduce SkillSpec, a two-phase framework comprising consensus-gated evolution and representation specialization. In the consensus-gated phase, complementary editing intents generate complete candidate skills. An update is committed only when paired evaluations reach consensus, requiring sufficient overall improvement and non-negative aggregate paired gain in every repeated evaluation. In the specialization phase, signals of process and redundancy sensitivity derived from the full optimization trajectory, including accepted and rejected candidates, guide the selection of a flat, graph, or hybridthis http URLsix benchmarks and three target language models, SkillSpec improves average success rate over SkillOpt by 6.89%, averaged across the three models. These results demonstrate that reliable skill evolution and representation specialization address complementary objectives: deciding what knowledge to retain and how to structure it for inference.
  </details>

- **[Accelerated Algorithm for Sparse Regularized Partial Optimal Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40075)**  `arXiv:2609.40075`  `cs.LG`  
  _Khoa Nguyen, Dung T. Nguyen, Thong Huynh, Hoang-Hiep Nguyen-Mau, Anh Nguyen, Minh Ngoc Dinh, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Partial Optimal Transport (POT) extends the classical optimal transport problem by relaxing the strict mass conservation constraint, enabling its use in a wide range of real-world applications. In many of these settings, sparse transport plans are preferred for their interpretability and computational benefits. While smooth and strongly convex regularizers - such as quadratic or elastic net - have been vastly used in various machine learning applications to induce sparsity and accelerate computation, they have received less algorithmic attention compared to entropic approaches for computational POT. In this paper, we propose a new optimization framework that leverages these regularizers through a penalty-based reformulation, enabling efficient gradient-based updates while preserving the structure of the original problem. Our method accommodates a broad class of regularizers that promote structured and sparse transport plans. Building on this formulation, we design an accelerated first-order algorithm that alternates between smooth updates and simple projection steps. Through empirical benchmarks on color transfer, domain adaptation, and point cloud registration, our approach consistently outperforms established baselines - achieving lower transport cost, higher sparsity, and faster convergence - making it a practical and scalable solution for modern transport problems.
  </details>

- **[PatchKV: Weight-Space Compensation of KV Cache](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39329)**  `arXiv:2609.39329`  `cs.LG`  
  _Chanryeol Lee, Chanhyuk Lee, Yeonwoo Choi, Donggyun Kim, Seunghoon Hong_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long-context inference with Large Language Models (LLMs) is bottlenecked by the linearly growing memory of the key-value (KV) cache. Existing compression methods reduce the cache through token eviction or approximation, but degrade sharply at aggressive compression budgets. We propose PatchKV, a training-free framework that compensates KV cache compression methods by carrying part of the context in the model's weights. PatchKV pairs an off-the-shelf compressed KV cache with a context-specific weight patch, which is computed once at context-loading time and served for downstream queries for the context. The weight patch is derived in closed form via ridge regression, by aligning the block-wise activations of context-derived reference query tokens under the full cache and the compressed cache. Once merged into the model, the patch leaves the forward graph and per-query inference cost unchanged in the single-context, multi-query setting. Across long-context QA (SCBench with up to 170K tokens, SQuAD, NIAH) and math (GSM8K) benchmarks on three model architectures, PatchKV consistently improves cache compression methods, suggesting an alternative direction to compensate them at aggressive budgets.
  </details>

- **[Koa-decision: Fast and Consistent Structured Decision Making with Generative LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36115)**  `arXiv:2609.36115`  `cs.LG`  
  _Shenghong Dai, Shiva Kumar Pentyala, Yingchi Liu, Shubham Mehrotra, Suman Banerjee, James Zhu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Industry applications often demand low-latency classification, yet current large language model (LLM) approaches remain poorly suited for latency-critical applications. Existing prompting and constrained decoding produce verbose, multi-token outputs that require expensive token-by-token generation, while encoder-based models achieve faster inference but sacrifice task flexibility. We propose Koa-decision, a framework for low-latency atomic actions -- fast, single-step decisions such as classification, semantic endpointing, Boolean checks, and scoring -- formulated as constrained generation with single-token outputs. By introducing atomic label tokens and applying supervised fine-tuning, our method reduces classification to a deterministic one-step decoding problem. Across standard benchmarks, Koa-decision delivers competitive accuracy with consistently low and stable latency. On a production intent-routing benchmark, Koa-decision reaches 85.5% accuracy -- competitive with the strongest frontier models (Claude-4.8-Opus, Gemini-Pro-3.1) and ahead of GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro -- while answering in about half a second, several-fold faster than every frontier model (up to ~7.5x at the median) under identical serving conditions. Against the dedicated single-token system Jev/TypeSafe, Koa-decision is competitive on accuracy and faster at the median, while also handling multimodal inputs and multi-label outputs that single-label text systems do not.
  </details>

- **[You Only Edit Once: Incentivizing In-Context Capability of LLMs via Local Demonstration Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33609)**  `arXiv:2609.33609`  `cs.LG`  
  _Jiarong Wen, Qi Wang, Yun Qu, Yixiu Mao, Heming Zou, Haoang Chi, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In-context learning (ICL) is crucial for boosting the inference performance of large language models (LLMs). However, the effectiveness of ICL in LLMs is greatly influenced by the choice of demonstration sets. Exhaustive searches over these sets are combinatorial, and existing selectors often rely on relevance or likelihood proxies to implicitly assess ICL quality. Making repeated queries to the target LLM with these strategies can incur substantial costs. This work simplifies selection by framing it as a constrained local search problem and presents local demonstration editing (LDE). Starting with an initially retrieved set of demonstrations, LDE employs a single structured edit to explore its surrounding neighborhood while balancing performance gains with search costs. Technically, LDE is reduced to a policy search problem, for which we train a small LLM, referred to as Jev-LDE. This model as the System-1 modifies the retrieved demonstration set by performing actions such as \texttt{Keep}, \texttt{Delete}, or \texttt{Replace} elements, all within a framework of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. At test time, Jev-LDE executes a single edit of the retrieved demonstration set, followed by one inference from the target LLM, avoiding the need for iterative context scoring or subset searches. Across standard classification benchmarks, various target LLMs with Jev-LDE as the plug-and-play module consistently improve ICL performance, and Jev-LDE shows transferability to held-out benchmarks and models without retraining. These findings indicate that the LDE approach offers an efficient and adaptable method for harnessing the ICL capabilities of target LLMs.
  </details>

- **[GeoACE: Geometry-Diverse Anchor-Correction Ensembles for Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29974)**  `arXiv:2609.29974`  `cs.LG`  
  _Ali Haghpanah Jahromi, Mohammad Taheri, Zohreh Azimifar_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Predicting heterogeneous causal effects supports informed decision-making, yet suitable inductive biases vary with treatment overlap, covariate imbalance, prognostic structure, and sample size. The Geometry-Diverse Anchor--Correction Expert Ensemble (GeoACE) addresses this variation through five complementary experts whose predictions are combined using weights estimated from validation data. Compared with ensemble designs that derive diversity primarily from sample or feature subsets, reweighting, or feature transformations, its central contribution is the coordinated design of training objectives and anchor geometries that target different prognostic and overlap structures. Following validation, each expert is refitted on the combined training and validation data, while retaining its distinctive structure. The shared architecture couples a structured outcome anchor with a learned neural correction. ACE serves as the reference estimator, while OW-ACE emphasizes well-supported covariate regions through overlap-weighted factual training. G$\Phi$-ACE constructs a global outcome-guided geometry from pooled prognostic associations, whereas A$\Phi$-ACE incorporates arm-specific outcome associations and penalties for treatment-group imbalance. O$\Phi$-ACE complements these approaches with an outcome-free, overlap-aware projection that replaces the anchor input with a lower-dimensional representation. GeoACE is evaluated against 11 comparators on eight benchmark protocols, alongside comparisons of weighting rules and aggregation controls. It achieves the lowest mean $\sqrt{\mathrm{PEHE}}$ and absolute average treatment effect error on all three IHDP protocols and closely approaches the best comparator on NEWS, although performance varies across the remaining benchmarks. The aggregation analyses show similar observed performance for inverse-DR weighting and equal averaging.
  </details>

- **[NAVIR: Neuromorphic Audio-Visual Speech Recognition for Robust Human-Robot Interaction on Edge Hardware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24391)**  `arXiv:2609.24391`  `cs.LG`  
  _Leonidas Delimpasis, Panagiota Moraiti, Antonis Porichis, Panos Chatzakos, Michail Karamousadakis_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Voice-controlled interaction in industrial settings is hampered by acoustic noise, which severely degrades audio-only speech recognition. Audio-visual speech recognition (AVSR) addresses this by fusing lip-motion cues with the audio stream, but state-of-the-art pipelines rely on three-dimensional convolutions, recurrent units, and attention modules that exceed the budget of typical edge devices. We present NAVIR, an end-to-end AVSR system targeting the BrainChip Akida neuromorphic processor, which natively supports only sequential two-dimensional convolutional inference. The pipeline factorises spatial and temporal encoding into separate AkidaNet-based modules: a per-frame visual encoder, a temporal video encoder, and a spectrogram audio encoder, fused by a lightweight predictor head and decoded by constrained beam search. Models are trained with connectionist temporal classification on noise-augmented audio and then fine-tuned with quantization-aware training. On the GRID benchmark, the quantized audio-visual model reaches 14.0% word error rate (WER) under noise on the unseen-speaker split and 3.3% WER on the overlapped-speaker split, against 22.5% and 11.8% for audio-only baselines, and it attains 98.6% command accuracy at 1.5% WER on a task-specific industrial-command corpus. Operation-count analysis indicates a 13-fold energy advantage of the spiking formulation over its artificial neural network counterpart at 27.6% mean firing rate. On-board measurements show roughly 5-fold lower energy per inference than a Raspberry Pi central processing unit on the lip-reading model, and over 100-fold lower than a laptop graphics processing unit, while sustaining 14.5 inferences per second. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first complete multimodal AVSR pipeline running on neuromorphic hardware of this class.
  </details>

- **[KV-Skill: Forging Expertise in the Model's Native Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05475)**  `arXiv:2608.05475`  `cs.LG`  
  _Zhaowei Han, Xiang Zhang, Bing Han, Kai Liu, Danqi Hu, Jie Liu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Task knowledge is commonly stored either as text in the prompt or as an update to model weights. Text is modular but must be interpreted on every use, while weight adaptation makes the resulting capability difficult to load, remove, or share independently. We introduce KV-Skill, a design space of external factorized operators that a frozen language model reads through a lightweight interface. KV-Skill supports two complementary paths. Registration converts an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and trains a shared per-backbone interface. Reward learning develops a compact latent operator directly from task outcomes, with or without an authored skill. Neither path adds positions to the prompt. Across ten benchmarks and four backbones from three model families, converting text to a KV-Skill consistently makes the same procedural knowledge more effective on mathematical reasoning and retrieval tasks. On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, registration reaches 77.2 accuracy, compared with 52.0 for the same skill as text (SkillOpt) and 64.5 for SoftSkill. Under matched reward training and parameter budgets, KV-Skill gives the best result in seven of eight matched settings against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA. A post-hoc rank analysis further shows that text-derived operators retain nearly all of their benefit with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while matched random directions fail. Finally, a single shared interface serves eleven diverse skills at once with no loss in average accuracy. These results show that task knowledge can be acquired from text or experience, compressed into an external operator, and deployed separately from the backbone. Code is available at:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Do You Even Need More Data? Rethinking LLM Deployment for Label-Scarce Tabular Classification with TabLens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24417)**  `arXiv:2605.24417`  `cs.LG`  
  _Daria Grushina, Kseniia Kuvshinova, Alina Kostromina, Aziz Temirkhanov, Mile Mitrovic, Dmitry Simakov_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Every tabular classification task requires sufficient labeled data. When labels are scarce, practitioners can collect more examples, encode domain expertise into features, or accept lower performance. Large language models offer an alternative by leveraging knowledge acquired during pretraining. This raises three questions: (i) can zero-shot inference reduce the need for labeled data; (ii) can a richer prompt reduce the need for more examples; and (iii) can encoded domain knowledge compensate for missing data? To answer each under explicit, testable conditions, we introduce TabLens, a benchmark of 91 real-world and synthetic datasets across eight domains, plus eight industrial datasets with free-text columns.First, below a complexity threshold estimable from a dataset's intrinsic dimensionality before running an LLM, zero-shot inference matches the accuracy of up to about 16 labeled examples. This holds whether the model generates an answer or, more cheaply, scores candidate labels by log-probabilities, which loses almost no accuracy except for the smallest models. Above the threshold, the advantage disappears. On datasets with free-text columns, however, zero-shot LLMs outperform 16-shot TabPFN-3 Plus without manual feature engineering. Second, a richer prompt reduces the number of required demonstrations only when it includes both real column names and a plain-language task description; providing only one can be worse than neither, particularly at higher shot counts. Third, on LLM-synthetic datasets, explicit if--then expert rules help only when the prompt provides enough task context to interpret them, and even then, they substitute for at most about 16 real examples. Together, these results establish testable conditions under which LLMs can reduce data-collection and feature-engineering requirements for tabular classification.
  </details>

- **[Do Deep Ensembles Actually Capture Uncertainty in Graph Neural Networks?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22593)**  `arXiv:2605.22593`  `cs.LG`  
  _Pedro C. Vieira, Pedro Ribeiro, Viacheslav Borovitskiy_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While deep ensembles are widely considered to be the default method for uncertainty quantification in deep learning, their effectiveness for graph-structured data is often simply assumed based on successes in domains like computer vision. We investigate standard deep ensembles specifically for message-passing graph neural networks. Benchmarking across eight datasets representing varied tasks and complexities, we reveal that ensembles provide only marginal improvement over a single model. These marginal gains stem primarily from averaging out optimization noise in point predictions rather than from meaningfully better uncertainty estimates.
