  </details>

- **[Q-Save: Towards Scoring and Attribution for Generated Video Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18825)**  `arXiv:2511.18825`  `cs.CV`  
  _Xiele Wu, Mingtao Chen, Zicheng Zhang, Yixian Liu, Yiming Liu, Jianxiang Lu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Evaluating AI-generated video (AIGV) quality hinges on three crucial dimensions: visual quality, dynamic quality, and text-video alignment. While numerous evaluation datasets and algorithms have been proposed, existing approaches are constrained by two limitations: the absence of systematic definitions for evaluation dimensions, and the isolated treatment of the three dimensions in separate models. Therefore, we introduce Q-Save, a holistic benchmark dataset and unified evaluation model for AIGV quality assessment. The Q-Save dataset contains nearly 10,000 video samples, each annotated with Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) and fine-grained attribution explanations across the three core dimensions. Leveraging this attribution-annotated dataset, we train the proposed Q-Save model, which adopts the SlowFast framework to balance accuracy and efficiency, and employs a three-stage training strategy with Chain-of-Thought (COT) formatted data: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Grouped Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and a final SFT round for stability, to jointly perform quality scoring and attribution generation. Experimental results demonstrate that Q-Save achieves superior performance in AIGV quality prediction while providing interpretable justifications. Code and dataset will be released upon publication.
  </details>

- **[ManipShield: A Unified Framework for Image Manipulation Detection, Localization and Explanation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14259)**  `arXiv:2511.14259`  `cs.CV`  
  _Zitong Xu, Huiyu Duan, Xiaoyu Wang, Zhaolin Cai, Kaiwei Zhang, Xiongkuo Min, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  With the rapid advancement of generative models, powerful image editing methods now enable diverse and highly realistic image manipulations that far surpass traditional deepfake techniques, posing new challenges for manipulation detection. Existing image manipulation detection and localization (IMDL) benchmarks suffer from limited content diversity, narrow generative-model coverage, and insufficient interpretability, which hinders the generalization and explanation capabilities of current manipulation detection methods. To address these limitations, we introduce \textbf{ManipBench}, a large-scale benchmark for image manipulation detection and localization focusing on AI-edited images. ManipBench contains over 450K manipulated images produced by 25 state-of-the-art image editing models across 12 manipulation categories, among which 100K images are further annotated with bounding boxes, judgment cues, and textual explanations to support interpretable detection. Building upon ManipBench, we propose \textbf{ManipShield}, an all-in-one model based on a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) that leverages contrastive LoRA fine-tuning and task-specific decoders to achieve unified image manipulation detection, localization, and explanation. Extensive experiments on ManipBench and several public datasets demonstrate that ManipShield achieves state-of-the-art performance and exhibits strong generality to unseen manipulation models. The project is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[From Classification to Cross-Modal Understanding: Leveraging Vision-Language Models for Fine-Grained Renal Pathology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.11984)**  `arXiv:2511.11984`  `cs.CV`  
  _Zhenhao Guo, Rachit Saluja, Tianyu Shi, Tianyuan Yao, Quan Liu, Junchao Zhu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Fine-grained glomerular subtyping is essential for kidney biopsy interpretation, yet it presents a harder setting than the broad organ- or disease-level recognition tasks commonly used in vision-language model (VLM) evaluation. In this task, all categories arise within the same renal microanatomic unit, and clinically meaningful subtypes often differ by subtle, overlapping, and continuum-like morphological cues. Clinically valuable labels are also scarce, making fully supervised image-only paradigms difficult to translate to practice. Although VLMs are promising for data-efficient pathology learning, it remains unclear how their cross-modal representations should be adapted and evaluated for such within-structure discrimination under realistic few-shot constraints. To our knowledge, this study establishes the first fine-grained renal pathology benchmark for few-shot VLM adaptation and systematically examines how supervision level, model design, and adaptation strategy shape both classification performance and multimodal representation structure. Beyond accuracy, AUC, and F1, we assess image-text alignment, positive-negative similarity separation, embedding geometry, and calibration (ECE), asking when performance gains reflect more reliable cross-modal understanding. Across renal pathology cohorts, additional supervision consistently improves discrimination, but reliable adaptation is not explained by alignment alone; stronger performance is associated with larger class separation, more coherent embedding organization, and better awareness of confidence-related failure modes under domain variation. Within this retrospective two-cohort evaluation, these findings move assessment beyond coarse classification and accuracy alone and provide comparative evidence to inform model selection and future translational validation. Code:this https URL
  </details>

- **[OmniRaindrop: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Dual-Focused Raindrop Removal under Day and Night Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17719)**  `arXiv:2510.17719`  `cs.CV`  
  _Zhiqiang Teng, Tingting Chen, Beibei Lin, Zifeng Yuan, Xuanyi Li, Xuanyu Zhang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Adherent raindrops on camera lenses are a pervasive source of real-world image degradation, undermining outdoor visual perception for downstream applications such as robotics and 3D scene reconstruction. However, most existing raindrop datasets and methods target only background-focused 2D images, overlooking the equally common raindrop-focused case and the impact of raindrops on 3D scene reconstruction. Moreover, they are almost exclusively daytime, lacking the complex artificial lighting and reflections of nighttime raindrop scenes. To address these issues, we introduce OmniRaindrop, a real-world dataset and benchmark that jointly evaluates 2D raindrop removal and 3D scene reconstruction across raindrop-focused and background-focused captures, under both daytime and nighttime conditions. OmniRaindrop provides spatially aligned raindrop-focused, background-focused, and rain-free ground-truth image sets: a 2D subset of 15,186 aligned pairs/triplets and a 3D subset of 40 real-world scenes evenly split between day and night, totaling 3,822 multi-view images. On top of this data, the benchmark traces how raindrop degradation propagates from 2D restoration to 3D reconstruction by testing representative restoration methods and their effects on pose estimation, point cloud initialization, and 3DGS optimization. Comprehensive experiments reveal that raindrop-focused scenes are substantially harder than background-focused ones, and that errors in 2D restoration and pose/point cloud initialization cascade into degraded 3D reconstruction, pointing to clear directions for more robust 2D restoration and 3DGS design. Building on the dataset, we have organized two consecutive NTIRE challenges (2025 and 2026) on Day and Night Raindrop Removal for Dual-Focused Images.
  </details>

- **[Universal Incremental Learning: Mitigating Confusion from Inter- and Intra-task Distribution Randomness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07035)**  `arXiv:2503.07035`  `cs.CV`  
  _Yi Zhou, Jinsong Shi, Sheng Luo, Tao Zhou_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Existing incremental learning (IL) methods rely on strong assumptions: incoming tasks either introduce exclusively new classes or new domains (i.e., Class IL and Domain IL), or increment by a fixed scale in a class- and domain-agnostic manner (i.e., Versatile IL, VIL). These assumptions severely limit their applicability in dynamic, unpredictable real-world scenarios. In this work, we investigate Universal Incremental Learning (UIL), a more realistic setting where the model has no prior knowledge of which new classes or domains will appear across sequential tasks, nor the scale of these increments within each task. This uncertainty hinders the model's ability to confidently acquire knowledge across varying task distributions and to learn uniformly from imbalanced intra-task distributions. Consequently, UIL introduces a more general IL scenario, where the model must cope with confusion stemming from both inter-task and intra-task distribution randomness. To mitigate both sources of confusion, we propose MiCo, a simple yet effective framework for UIL. At the inter-task level, we employ a multi-objective learning scheme to enforce accurate and deterministic predictions, further enhanced by a direction recalibration module that alleviates conflicting gradient updates. At the intra-task level, we introduce a magnitude recalibration module to address asymmetrical optimization caused by imbalanced class distributions. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate that MiCo significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both the proposed UIL and existing VIL scenarios.
  </details>

- **[Encoding Context into LLM Weights: What Makes It Context?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17686)**  `arXiv:2610.17686`  `cs.CL` `cs.LG`  
  _Yue Wang, Qizhou Wang, Feng Liu, Gang Niu, Masashi Sugiyama, Bo Han_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Longer contexts allow large language models (LLMs) to condition their predictions on more information, but inference costs grow prohibitively with context length. An emerging alternative uses test-time updates to encode context as temporary changes to model weights. However, encoding this information into weights that already represent general knowledge obscures its role as context, so the LLM may fail to use it properly to condition subsequent inference. To restore this contextual role, we first associate each context with an identifier during encoding, thereby distinguishing the newly encoded information from pre-existing knowledge. Invoking the identifier at inference then enables the LLM to recite the encoded context. Nevertheless, successful recitation does not ensure that the LLM will use the recalled information as context. We therefore further introduce a prompting framework that explicitly guides the LLM to use this information as context. Across diverse controlled tasks and practical benchmarks, our method outperformed the baseline using only off-the-shelf LLMs, showing its advances in context encoding.
  </details>

- **[Think Before You Speak: Enabling Training-Free Latent Communication Between Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16165)**  `arXiv:2610.16165`  `cs.CL` `cs.LG`  
  _Rishi Khare_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks in coding, mathematical logic, and iterative reasoning, especially by coordinating effectively within multi-agent systems (MAS). However, language agents traditionally communicate via text exchange, which introduces a bottleneck in information transfer and adds prefill latency for downstream agents. Recent work proposes that directly sharing the key-value (KV) cache between language models can enable efficient latent collaboration, entirely bypassing standard text-based communication. To enable latent communication between heterogeneous models of different sizes, prior work introduces trained fusion adapters for each model pair, which limits practical deployment. We introduce CacheFuse, a training-free method which demonstrates that augmenting a downstream model with an upstream model's KV cache using linear interpolation consistently enables superior performance than the standalone downstream model can achieve. We systematically analyze CacheFuse across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks and demonstrate up to 8.6 percentage points higher accuracy compared to single-model baselines and up to 12.2x TTFT speedup compared to text-based communication in multi-model inference.
  </details>

- **[Sanzaru: Benchmarking Protocol Formation under Epistemic & Communication Asymmetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15163)**  `arXiv:2610.15163`  `cs.CL` `cs.LG`  
  _Yiping Li, Zhiyu An, Wan Du_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A language model's ability to solve a task individually does not ensure that a team can solve it under unequal access to information and communication. SANZARU examines this gap through cooperative bomb-defusal puzzles adapted from BOMBANANA! (Lefto Studio, 2026). Task information and action authority are divided among three agents: one cannot hear, another cannot speak, and the third cannot see. The benchmark contains 120 puzzle instances across seven families, each targeting a distinct coordination ability. Across 1512 episodes, 7 models achieve an overall success rate of 49%, ranging from 20% to 86% under the evaluated configurations. Teams develop or adopt diverse communication protocols, from simple gesture codes to Morse and encodings of entire manuals. Yet trace analysis attributes about 60% of 771 team losses to communication, and agents attempt to use channels unavailable to their teammates despite explicit role instructions. Together, task outcomes and interaction traces enable evaluation of both collaborative performance and perspective taking throughout cooperation. The benchmark is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[LLM Persona Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39882)**  `arXiv:2609.39882`  `cs.CL` `cs.LG`  
  _Kemou Li, Zhuan Shi, Qizhou Wang, Fengpeng Li, Negar Rostamzadeh, Golnoosh Farnadi, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Pre-training equips large language models (LLMs) with a broad repertoire of behavioral patterns associated with roles, styles, values, and goals. Post-training teaches conditional enactment and makes a helpful Assistant the default, but it does not erase alternative modes from the weights; explicit prompts can therefore elicit personas that repeatedly shape judgment, language, and action. In open-weight settings, runtime controls can be removed, motivating persona unlearning: a weight-level edit that makes a designated persona difficult to elicit and enact on unseen contexts. We introduce PersonaUnlearnBench, a model-specific paired benchmark spanning six LLMs from three families and five personas, with aligned forget/retain sets, held-out instruction paraphrases, and four-axis evaluation. The benchmark shows that standard unlearning methods cannot reliably erase the target persona without sacrificing meaningful generation or general utility. We therefore propose PaCE, which compares target and desirable responses to the same questions to locate an internal behavior direction, then trains target-prompt states away from the target mode and toward the matched desirable response. Experiments show that PaCE consistently suppresses target personas with high response quality and useful counterpart behavior, at moderate utility cost. These results establish persona unlearning as a distinct behavior-level editing problem and a practical route toward persistent control of latent LLM response policies.
  </details>

- **[Monitoring and Discovering Reward Hacking with Internal Representations during LLM Evaluations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19101)**  `arXiv:2609.19101`  `cs.CL` `cs.LG`  
  _Leon Bergen, Usha Bhalla, Andrew Lee, Barak Widawsky, Linas Nasvytis, Connor Watts, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As models scale, reward hacking becomes more frequent, more sophisticated, and more consequential. Does it leave a telltale signature in model representations? This work analyzes how reward hacking is represented internally in frontier open source LLMs, and how those representations can be used to understand and discover the range of hacking behaviors a model displays. In particular, we find that simple difference of means vectors coherently represent reward hacking in Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, and Qwen 3.8 Max across a variety of behaviors in common evaluations. Despite their simplicity, these vectors are both generalizable and interpretable, and we can use them to reliably detect reward hacking. We first evaluate reward hacking in commonly reported benchmarks like DeepSWE and SWE-bench, finding that models reward hack excessively in these environments; GLM 5.2 hacks in 57.2% of rollouts on DeepSWE and in 73% of rollouts on SWE-bench. Catching these requires monitors; LLM monitors are effective, but expensive detectors. We show that DoM vectors are similarly effective but virtually free, catching 3.1% more hacks in Kimi K3 and 7.9% fewer hacks in GLM 5.2 on DeepSWE at a monitor matched false positive rate. DoM vectors run on the chain-of-thought also predict reward hacks in the model's subsequent actions, meaning we can run them online and catch potential hacks before they occur. Finally, we analyze probe-hits that LLM monitors do not catch and discover other undesirable behaviors, as well as show transfer to finding hacks in non-SWE evaluations. Together, these results provide evidence that simple, white-box methods can be used to scalably study and monitor reward hacking behaviors in frontier open source models
  </details>

- **[Planner-Guided Recursive Exploration for Diffusion Language Model Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15655)**  `arXiv:2607.15655`  `cs.CL` `cs.LG`  
  _Yingqian Cui, Wei Deng, Lantao Mei, Hang Li, Charu C. Aggarwal, Hui Liu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Masked diffusion language models (DLMs) enable parallel text generation by iteratively refining masked tokens, offering a promising alternative to autoregressive decoding. Recent search-based decoding methods improve the accuracy--efficiency trade-off by exploring multiple candidate decoding trajectories before committing token updates. However, existing search-based decoding methods face two key limitations. First, they offer limited guidance on when search is actually beneficial for the current decoding state. Second, they typically rely on a shallow one-step search horizon, which may favor locally promising but suboptimal decoding trajectories. To address these limitations, we propose PRED, a planner-guided recursive exploration framework for DLM decoding. PRED employs a learned planner to determine when search should be triggered, and performs adaptive multi-step rollout to evaluate candidate trajectories over longer horizons. Moreover, the same planner is recursively applied to intermediate rollout states to determine whether additional branch expansion is needed, allowing PRED to re-initiate search when necessary. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and DLM backbones show that PRED achieves a better accuracy--efficiency trade-off than existing confidence-based and search-based decoding methods.
  </details>

- **[BehaviorBench: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Behavioral Science Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24162)**  `arXiv:2606.24162`  `cs.CL` `cs.LG`  
  _Jin Huang, Yutong Xie, Wanli Song, Xingjian Zhang, Owen Yang, Walter Yuan, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Foundation models have been increasingly applied to behavioral science domains such as psychology, sociology, and economics. While these models show promise in tasks such as survey response prediction and human-subject experiment simulation, there remains no systematic understanding of how well they perform across diverse behavioral science tasks. We introduce BehaviorBench, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates foundation models along four core capabilities: (1) behavior prediction and simulation, (2) strategic decision-making, (3) subject-trait inference, and (4) behavioral knowledge application. Crucially, BehaviorBench evaluates model outputs at both the individual and distributional levels, capturing not only per-subject accuracy but also population-level alignment, an essential requirement for behavioral validity. Our evaluation shows that BehaviorBench remains challenging for leading general-purpose LLMs and behavior foundation models that are specifically trained with behavioral data. We find that individual-level and distributional performance do not always align. General-purpose LLMs tend to underestimate the diversity of human responses, whereas behavior foundation models often lag behind at individual-level prediction. Our investigation further demonstrates how fine-tuning on diverse behavioral data can improve both individual-level prediction and distributional alignment, balancing these two objectives. Our results highlight the importance of evaluation at both individual and distributional levels, establishing BehaviorBench as a foundation for developing and assessing behaviorally aligned AI systems. Our BehaviorBench and models can be accessed viathis https URL
  </details>

- **[ControBench: An Interaction-Aware Benchmark for Controversial Discourse Analysis on Social Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00513)**  `arXiv:2605.00513`  `cs.CL` `cs.LG`  
  _Ta Thanh Thuy, Jiaqi Zhu, Xuan Liu, Lin Shang, Reihaneh Rabbany, Guillaume Rabusseau, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Understanding how people argue across ideological divides online is important for studying political polarization, misinformation, and content moderation. Existing datasets capture only part of this problem: some preserve text but ignore interaction structure, some model structure without rich semantics, and others represent conversations without stable user-level ideological identity. We introduce ControBench, a benchmark for controversial discourse analysis that combines heterogeneous social interaction graphs with rich textual semantics. Built from Reddit discussions on three topics, Trump, abortion, and religion, ControBench contains 7,370 users, 1,783 posts, and 26,525 interactions. The graph contains user and post nodes connected by semantically enriched edges; in particular, user-comment-user edges encode both a reply and the parent comment that it responds to, preserving local argumentative context. User labels are derived from self-declared Reddit flairs, providing a scalable proxy for ideological identity without manual annotation. The resulting datasets exhibit low or negative adjusted homophily (Trump: -0.77, Abortion: 0.06, Religion: 0.04), reflecting the cross-cutting structure of real-world debate. We evaluate graph neural networks, pretrained language models, and large language models on ControBench and observe distinct performance patterns across topics and model families, especially when ideological boundaries are ambiguous. These results position ControBench as a challenging and realistic benchmark for controversial discourse analysis.
  </details>

- **[An Agentic AI System for Multi-Framework Communication Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08659)**  `arXiv:2512.08659`  `cs.CL` `cs.LG`  
  _Bohao Yang, Rui Yang, Joshua M. Biro, Haoyuan Wang, Jessica L. Handley, Brianna N. Richardson, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Clinical communication is central to patient outcomes, yet large-scale human annotation of patient-provider conversation remains labor-intensive, inconsistent, and difficult to scale. Existing approaches based on large language models typically rely on single-task models that lack adaptability, interpretability, and reliability, especially when applied across various communication frameworks and clinical domains. In this study, we developed a Multi-framework Structured Agentic AI system for Clinical Communication (MOSAIC), built on a LangGraph-based architecture that orchestrates four core agents, including a Plan Agent for codebook selection and workflow planning, an Update Agent for maintaining up-to-date retrieval databases, a set of Annotation Agents that applies codebook-guided retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with dynamic few-shot prompting, and a Verification Agent that provides consistency checks and feedback. To evaluate performance, we compared MOSAIC outputs against gold-standard annotations created by trained human coders. We developed and evaluated MOSAIC using 26 gold standard annotated transcripts for training and 50 transcripts for testing, spanning rheumatology and OB/GYN domains. On the test set, MOSAIC achieved an overall F1 score of 0.928. Performance was highest in the Rheumatology subset (F1 = 0.962) and strongest for Patient Behavior (e.g., patients asking questions, expressing preferences, or showing assertiveness). Ablations revealed that MOSAIC outperforms baseline benchmarking.
  </details>

- **[PVFH-Bench: Benchmarking Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14635)**  `arXiv:2610.14635`  `cs.CL` `cs.CV`  
  _Xinhao Wang, Junbo Cui, Zhenghao Liu, Yuan Yao, Xiaohua Li, Yu Gu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across a wide range of multimodal tasks. However, object hallucination remains a persistent challenge, undermining model reliability in applications such as visual question answering, embodied agents, and human-AI decision support systems. In this paper, inspired by cognitive science studies on perceptual bias, we investigate a new failure mode termed Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination (PVFH). Specifically, PVFH refers to a premise-induced reasoning error in which models become anchored to visually confusable evidence, accept a false textual premise, and subsequently generate responses about an absent yet visually plausible object. To systematically study this phenomenon, we introduce PVFH-Bench, a benchmark that automatically constructs visually confusable but absent targets and pairs the core hallucination setting with diagnostic subsets to trace how models move from object recognition to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Experimental results on 10 state-of-the-art LVLMs demonstrate that all evaluated models are highly vulnerable to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Moreover, we find that explicit chain-of-thought reasoning can further exacerbate this failure mode by encouraging models to overinterpret weak visual cues as supporting evidence for hallucinated objects.
  </details>

- **[DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18862)**  `arXiv:2610.18862`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Minghao Luo, Liang Chen_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Hybrid Reasoning Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18861)**  `arXiv:2610.18861`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Jiaru Zou, Yunzhe Qi, Sirui Chen, Federico Bianchi, Shang Zhu, Pan Lu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Agaram 2.5B: The First Tamil-First Language Model Trained from Scratch with Tool Calling. A Playbook for Under-Represented Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18420)**  `arXiv:2610.18420`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`

  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We trained Agaram 2.5B, a 2.5-billion-parameter Tamil-English language model, from scratch on about 50 billion tokens (58% Tamil, the rest English, math, code and parallel text) on one node of eight H100 GPUs in about six days, with a new tokenizer that, unlike our first model's, keeps line breaks. Supervised fine-tuning on 134,428 conversations, whose replies an open-weight teacher model wrote, and three short targeted rounds turned it into a chat model that answers in Tamil script, romanized Tamil (Tanglish) and English and can call tools: on 25 tool prompts whose schemas appear in training it picks the right tool 23 times and gives exactly the expected arguments 13 times. The released model translates better than Sarvam-1, a 2B Indic base model, in all six FLORES and IN22 directions (FLORES chrF 54.3 into Tamil and 55.2 into English, against 49.2 and 44.2), and nearly doubles its base model on native-Tamil IndicIFEval (19.3% from 10.0%). It is weak on knowledge: reading-comprehension and knowledge benchmarks sit near chance, and on 50 held-out everyday questions written by one native speaker, one LLM judge rated 46% of its replies usable (22-24 of 50 over three passes; 95% interval for 23 of 50, 33-60%), with nearly every failure a wrong fact. Our two further SFT experiments changed answer format but not the knowledge measures. We also describe our first model, Agaram 1.5B, whose failures shaped the choices here; how the judge's scores varied between passes on identical replies; and, item by item, what the targeted rounds trained against and where frontier-model text entered the data. The project ran on compute credits and our own funds, about USD 13,300 across both models; the weights are released (licence to be announced after legal review), with GGUF files forthis http URL, atthis https URLcode atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Auditing Failure Attribution: Label Predictability and Judge Behavior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17747)**  `arXiv:2610.17747`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Tianyang Xu, Jing Gao_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Failure-attribution benchmarks ask an LLM judge which step or agent caused a failure. A high score should mean the judge checked the faulty step against the run (a cross-step check). However, spurious signals (surface cues) that predict the annotation can produce a high score. In this paper, we propose four tests to separate checking from cue use. Input restriction asks whether partial input predicts the annotation. Cue following checks whether moved cues change answers. Residual accuracy scores judges where cue-only predictors fail. Aggregation asks whether the failure mix or metric changes rankings. Real observations motivate these tests: on three benchmarks, simple predictors match or beat GPT-4.1. In two Who&When Pro systems, a classifier reading one step's reasoning finds 95-100% of faulty steps, motivating input restriction. In one of them, error injection leaves no reasoning after the faulty step; judges fine-tuned on its labels beat GPT-4.1 by 41 points. Adding task-related reasoning after that step moves this cue: fine-tuned judges lose 31-99 points, but zero-shot judges lose at most 9, motivating cue following. On Aegis, blaming every agent matches GPT-4.1 on micro-F1 but trails by 19 points in exact-set accuracy, motivating aggregation. We recommend reporting these tests when developing failure-attribution benchmarks.
  </details>

- **[LatentRiskBench: Measuring State-Dependent Risks in Enterprise Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17685)**  `arXiv:2610.17685`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Jingyue Cong, Estrid He, Zhuang Li, Nan Wu, Li Shen, Yameng Peng, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Enterprise agents face safety risks that cannot be determined from individual actions alone. Existing safety benchmarks largely evaluate action-local risks, overlooking failures whose safety depends on workflow state. In such state-dependent risks, the same action may be safe in one context but violate policy in another. Hence, we introduce LatentRiskBench for evaluating such state-dependent risks in enterprise settings. It pairs risky trajectories with benign counterparts that share the same terminal action but differ in latent policy-relevant states, requiring models to reconstruct workflow context rather than rely on action-level cues. We also introduce new metrics for state-dependent risk evaluation, including a suite of residual risk (RR) measures. Experiments on the benchmark show that action-level evaluation detects only 0.09 of state-dependent violations, whereas state-level evaluation reaches 0.96. Existing guardrail methods largely overlook such risks unless they are explicitly applied to workflow states. Case studies on a commercial deployed scenario further show that the safety metrics embedded in the benchmark provide a more realistic measure of safety for enterprise agents. Our dataset and code are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Compositional RL: Evaluating and Training LLMs for Collaborative Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17456)**  `arXiv:2610.17456`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Shangbin Feng, Yulia Tsvetkov, Jan Kautz, David Acuna_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Language models are often evaluated alone but increasingly deployed together, routed between, made to debate, ensembled, or collaboratively trained. For a model inside a system, what matters most is not how well it performs on its own, but how much the system gains from its presence. We call this a model's compositional strength and formalize it using the Shapley value of a cooperative game over coalitions of a model pool, and use a model's leave-one-out contribution to the full coalition as a tractable proxy, requiring n+1 rather than 2^n system evaluations. Evaluating individual vs. compositional strengths across five model pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets, we find them largely uncorrelated: in 12 of 15 (pool, method-family) settings, individual strength does not translate into compositional advantages, and the coupling is weakest among general-purpose models that practitioners are most likely to deploy. Standalone benchmarks are therefore often poor proxies for models' value in collaborative systems. We then propose compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL), which trains a policy inside a live multi-model system and rewards the outcome produced by the system as a whole, rather than the policy's correctness in isolation. The leave-one-out baseline in Shapley values cancels under a group policy gradient, so this needs no additional rollout cost beyond RL on the collaborative system's outcome and never requires running a coalition without the policy. Across three collaboration protocols and eight tasks spanning reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery, C-RL produces the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings, lifting collaborative performance by +4.0 to +5.4 pts on average (~3x the gain of baselines), up to +13.1 pts.
  </details>

- **[Sensitivity or Criterion? Measuring and Moving When Language Models Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15415)**  `arXiv:2610.15415`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Sixun Dong, Yebowen Hu, Ming Yin, Yiran Chen, Fei Liu, Chen Chen_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Before an agent acts, it must decide whether action is warranted. A single accuracy cannot distinguish failure to recognize a warranted action from reluctance to act. Signal-detection theory separates sensitivity from criterion, but criteria estimated from authored binary labels depend on each benchmark's example mix. We introduce FlipAct, a diagnostic of tool use in physical states. A rule over annotated tool properties computes each answer and a graded evidence score, fixing the Yes/No boundary at zero across models. Questions form 2-by-2 quads that hold required knowledge fixed while the state flips. The slope of the fitted Yes-rate curve measures sensitivity; its crossing at one half measures criterion. Across 44 open models, sensitivity rises with size within a family, and its ranking agrees with three of four external when-to-act benchmarks. Models respond to evidence sign rather than magnitude, accepting actions that leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones. When Yes means act, most models are conservative across rephrasings; in some, this partly reflects a preference for No. Criterion is not determined by size. Activation steering shifts criterion with weights fixed; distillation from a model's own steered copy puts the shift into its weights without a significant sensitivity change. The distilled shift transfers to six external benchmarks, including two without Yes/No answers, while criterion-free AUC is preserved on the five benchmarks where it is available. Accuracy improves where models start conservative and declines or remains within error where they start permissive. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Agentic Data Engineering for LLMs: System Design and a Controlled Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14238)**  `arXiv:2610.14238`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Ruomeng Ding, Qianli Shen, Zhaoyang Han, Meixin Chen, Daoyuan Chen, Yaliang Li_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM data engineering requires iterative experimentation to determine how data selection, rewards, and curricula affect model learning, making it a natural setting for AI-for-AI (AI4AI) research. Can agents use experimental feedback to progressively improve strategies, and do the resulting strategies improve target-model performance on held-out data? We study how agents use experimental feedback to develop data-engineering strategies under fixed training and evaluation protocols. Our Agentic Data Engineering (ADE) framework lets agents pursue, revise, or combine research directions using cumulative findings. Strategies are selected by in-loop scores and evaluated on held-out benchmarks. Across four tasks-math and code data selection, math reward design, and math curriculum learning-selected strategies achieve absolute gains over generic baselines of up to 13.34% on AIME25 Pass@32 and 5.85% averaged across four held-out benchmarks under fixed training conditions. In-loop scores improve over successive experiments, while held-out trajectories show that later in-loop gains do not always improve generalization. Comparisons of research organization and feedback access favor combining evidence analysis with cumulative findings. Research trajectories show how earlier findings inform strategy revisions and combinations across research directions.
  </details>

- **[One Size Does Not Fit All: Distribution-Guided Tensor-Wise Adaptive Sparsification for Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06163)**  `arXiv:2508.06163`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Yingfeng Luo, Dingyang Lin, Junxin Wang, Kaiyan Chang, Ziqiang Xu, Weiqiao Shan, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Merging multiple task-specific fine-tuned checkpoints into a single multi-task model provides an attractive alternative to joint multi-task training. To mitigate cross-task interference, a common strategy is to sparsify task vectors before aggregation. However, many widely used methods rely on a uniform global sparsity ratio, overlooking differences in pruning sensitivity across tasks and parameter tensors. Consequently, such uniform sparsification may remove useful parameter updates from sensitive tensors while retaining redundant updates in others. To address this limitation, we propose TADrop, a plug-and-play sparsifier that independently determines tensor-specific keep ratios from their magnitude distributions using a scale-invariant quantile ratio. TADrop operates in a data-free manner by default, while offering optional lightweight module-level calibration when a small validation set is available. Experiments across vision, language, and multimodal benchmarks, including LLM and LoRA merging, demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple host merging methods, including a 4.99-point gain over EMR-Merging on RoBERTa GLUE. In many-task ViT-B/16 merging, the improvement increases with the number of tasks, reaching 2.26 points when merging 30 tasks. Further analyses show that TADrop preserves more task-associated neurons under matched overall sparsity. Together, these findings highlight the value of distribution-guided sparsification at the tensor level for improving model merging.
  </details>

- **[RCStat: A Statistical Framework for using Relative Contextualization in Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19549)**  `arXiv:2506.19549`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Debabrata Mahapatra, Shubham Agarwal, Apoorv Saxena, Subrata Mitra_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Identifying which tokens and activations truly influence model predictions is critical for both the efficiency and interpretability of large auto-regressive language models. Yet in practice, token importance is typically inferred from attention distributions that entangle contextual relevance with softmax-normalization effects, obscuring relative influence across tokens and heads. We propose $\textbf{RCStat}$, a statistical framework for quantifying contextual influence in attention mechanisms. At its core $\textbf{Relative Contextualization (RC)}$ is a random variable that measures how strongly one subset of tokens contributes to another under the model's internal scoring scheme. RCStat admits computationally efficient bounds on expected influence that can be estimated at inference time. No retraining is required. We apply RCStat to two tasks. For $\textbf{attribution}$, attention heads with high expected RC accurately identify the prompt spans that drive generation, enabling reliable span-level explanations. For $\textbf{key-value cache eviction}$, RC-based adaptive thresholding selectively evicts low-impact KV entries, substantially reducing cache size while preserving generation quality. Across question answering, summarization, and attribution benchmarks, RCStat achieves consistent gains, improving generation quality by 15-40% with upto 36% error reduction for KV eviction, and attribution accuracy by 2-16%. These results demonstrate that explicitly modeling contextual influence provides a principled and practical alternative to attention-based heuristics.
  </details>

- **[Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18868)**  `arXiv:2610.18868`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.CV` `cs.LG`  
  _Wenbo Hu, Shraman Pramanick, Krishna Kumar Singh, Nanyun Peng, Kai-Wei Chang, Yong Jae Lee_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents' Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.
  </details>

- **[Jev-ToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Typed Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18610)**  `arXiv:2610.18610`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Kawai Chung, Chunkit Chan, Yuxuan Liu, Yauwai Yim, Xi Yang, Wenbin Hu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. TypeSafe Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy including native controls and ranks first or second across all six capabilities, leading beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, and emotions. Other typed models show distinct strengths across tasks. Separate resource comparisons suggest that Jev could reduce the cost and waiting time of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons can repair errors or overturn correct answers depending on their attachment. Candidate expansion reveals distinct selection and output-validity problems. Related-question cues account for most of Jev's downstream gains, with task-dependent effects from predicted states. The findings motivate testing Jev as a ToM selection component in assistants, with task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation as integration priorities.
  </details>

- **[Aligning Faithfulness for Theory-Scale Autoformalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18498)**  `arXiv:2610.18498`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Yuming Feng, Tadd Mao, Dhruva Arekar, Tianjun Zhong, Jiani Huang, Xujie Si, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Autoformalization (AF) requires more than compilation: formal statements must preserve the meaning of their informal sources, a property known as faithfulness. An emerging frontier is the automated evaluation of this property, yet most existing methods operate at the statement level and produce whole-item verdicts, failing to reveal how individual expressions correspond or which contextual interpretations support the judgment. This omission is consequential because AF is inherently theory-scale: target statements derive their meaning from surrounding mathematical material and unstated conventions. We formulate faithfulness evaluation as a context-aware align-then-label problem: identifying phrase-level correspondences between informal and formal statements and assigning a faithfulness label to each under explicitly specified contextual interpretations and assumptions. We also introduce FaithAlign, the first theory-scale faithfulness benchmark comprising 460 items and 4,982 annotated phrase-level links, alongside FaithAlign-Gap, a companion set of 146 items with informal context and assumptions withheld. Each FaithAlign item includes the target statement pair, relevant context, formal dependencies, and, where needed, assumptions specifying one given interpretation. Across 8 models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest defect F1 at 47.8% and identifies all defects in only 4.5% of items with two or more defects. On FaithAlign-Gap, Astra identifies only 28.2% of undecidable items as such. These results show the difficulty of recovering context-dependent correspondences, establishing FaithAlign as a testbed for fine-grained, context-aware faithfulness evaluation.
  </details>

- **[Do Factuality Methods Make LLMs More Factual? Reproducibility and Fair Comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18415)**  `arXiv:2610.18415`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Pratuat Amatya, Vinay Setty, V Venktesh, Avishek Anand_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to human preferences, after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning steps. However, standard RL alignment steps such as RLHF do not focus on factuality of LLMs, hence they may generate non-factual information, which could result in unintended consequences. In response, a number of factuality alignment approaches have been proposed in the literature which claim to improve factuality of LLMs on their own benchmarks. However, these methods have not been reproduced independently and are also not comparable since each uses a different base model, training data, evaluation set, judge, and metric. In this paper, we present the first independent reproduction of five factuality alignment methods, which span on-policy RL (PPO, GRPO, and Dr.~GRPO) and offline preference optimization (DPO and KTO), and compare them on a common benchmark with common evaluation metrics. We found that none of these methods reproduces in full, and on the common benchmark none of the methods significantly outperforms the base model. On closer inspection, the rewards optimize for format, length, or brevity rather than factuality and relevance, whereas the choice between on-policy and offline training matters little. Furthermore, the evaluation metrics and benchmarks are also part of the problem since they do not measure relevance of text to the prompt. Since there is no ground truth associated with the prompts, the reliance on LLM judges and retrieval for verification also makes the evaluation fragile. We release our code, data, and checkpoints.
  </details>

- **[Lightweight but Linguistically Fair? Quantisation Robustness across Bavarian, German, and English](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18343)**  `arXiv:2610.18343`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Jophin John, Michael Hoffmann, Piroska Lendvai, Florent Dufour_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Post-training quantisation reduces the memory cost of large language models, but it remains unclear whether compression preserves language skills of regional varieties as reliably as their standard-language counterparts. We study this question for Bavarian, Standard German, and English using BAVGROUND, a multiple-choice benchmark, where 206 source questions are aligned across all three languages. Across 14 open-weight 7B--10B instruction models, we compare BF16 with 8-bit GPTQ and two 4-bit settings, GPTQ and AWQ. Eight-bit GPTQ remains close to BF16 and largely preserves the relative behaviour of the three languages, while 4-bit quantisation was found to be much less stable. The two 4-bit methods reduce average accuracy by about 1.4--1.5 percentage points and change 11.9--16.0% of BF16 decisions, with changes concentrated on examples where the BF16 model is already uncertain. This instability does not translate into a consistent Bavarian disadvantage. Although Bavarian, a low-resource dialect, has lower baseline accuracy than German and English, the language most affected at 4 bits varies across models and quantisation methods. Calibration further shapes these cross-language effects: the relative Bavarian--German effect changes with calibration language, while changing the calibration source has little average effect on GPTQ-4 but can affect AWQ-4 much more strongly. Free-form evaluation on five models further shows that 4-bit compression can degrade generated responses even in settings where multiple-choice accuracy changes only modestly, while 8-bit GPTQ remains comparatively stable. Overall, our results show that quantisation robustness for regional language varieties depends on the model, quantisation method, calibration data, and evaluation setting, and cannot be measured by aggregate multilingual accuracy alone.
  </details>

- **[TextualRL: Textual Reinforcement Learning for Context Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18216)**  `arXiv:2610.18216`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Tianyu Huai, Jie Zhou, Bo Mao, Qin Chen, Liang He, Xipeng Qiu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM agents can adapt to task feedback by revising the textual context that guides their behavior, without changing their model parameters. However, turning execution rewards into reusable context updates is challenging: individual trajectories offer limited comparative evidence about what to change, while task-specific fixes may overgeneralize when incorporated into a shared context. We introduce TextualRL, a gradient-free reinforcement learning framework that treats a group of rollouts from the same task under the same context, rather than an isolated trajectory, as the unit of policy critique. Groupwise Policy Critique contrasts successful and failed rollouts within a task; when outcomes are uniform, it draws on cross-task evidence to identify behaviors worth preserving or formulate repair hypotheses. Cross-Group Policy Update reviews the resulting proposals against evidence pooled across groups, including observations that yield no proposed edit, to refine their content and applicability. Reviewed proposals form a bounded textual patch, with adoption of the candidate context determined by held-out validation rewards. Together, these components establish a reward-driven policy optimization loop in which multiple attempts jointly inform reusable context updates. We evaluate TextualRL with five target agents on six benchmarks. Averaged over the six benchmarks, TextualRL improves test accuracy over the base model by 24.4 and 15.3 percentage points for GPT-5.5 and Qwen3.8-27B, respectively.
  </details>

- **[Virtual Head Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17959)**  `arXiv:2610.17959`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Xibo Ding, Guoxia Wang, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Sirui Tao, Chao Yang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale ($+$0.05\% to $+$0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by $4\times$ vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and $2\times$ vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, $S{=}4096$). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by $+$0.70\,/\,$+$2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.
  </details>

- **[StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17309)**  `arXiv:2610.17309`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Xialie Zhuang, Zunhai Su, Jia Pan, Ngai Wong, Guanhua Chen, Chuan-Wei Kuo_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce StartLux-Decision, decision models from 0.8B to 27B parameters that combine efficient single-pass prediction with adaptive, confidence-guided reasoning. The Instant models use bidirectional attention in full-attention layers to improve decision accuracy while keeping single-pass inference. The AutoThink models invoke explicit reasoning for uncertain decisions and answer confident cases directly. A three-stage training pipeline establishes shared decision capabilities, specializes the two variants, and equips AutoThink with reasoning through reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning. We introduce Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions (RLCD$^2$), which uses a frozen model and proper scoring rules to reward improvements in decision probability quality and applies a soft penalty to overlong reasoning traces. RLCD$^2$ raises the share of reasoning traces that terminate within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and cuts average reasoning length by up to 65%, while largely preserving decision accuracy. On the public subset of Decision Index 0.3, the Instant models outperform the strongest evaluated comparable-scale open-weight decision models by 7.4-16.9 points, and the 27B AutoThink model reaches 73.4. We also introduce DecisionPivot, a programmatically verifiable benchmark of computational decisions built from contrast pairs that differ in a single answer-changing detail. On DecisionPivot, AutoThink outperforms its Instant counterparts by 11.5-18.4 points in pair accuracy and leads among evaluated systems. The models run on vLLM,this http URLand MLX, with quantized variants for lower memory use.
  </details>

- **[Calibrated Typed Decisions for Entity, Relation, and Event Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17113)**  `arXiv:2610.17113`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Yang Wang, Hanlin Xiao, Yanan Ma, Chenghao Xiao, Chenghua Lin_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Information extraction models often perform well on the datasets they are trained on, but transferring to new domains and annotation guidelines remains challenging. Supporting user-specified types alone does not resolve this problem. We present CalOn, a unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for entity, relation, and event extraction across datasets and schemas. The model jointly encodes text and type definitions, then directly identifies entity spans, relations between spans, and event triggers and arguments. Its extraction decisions consider the requested types together, using their combined evidence to identify relevant candidates before assigning a type. This gives all three tasks a common probabilistic formulation while keeping every extracted mention anchored to the input text. We train on diverse sources, and supplement supervised learning with a reward that encourages correct extractions and penalises incorrect ones. Across 40 benchmarks, CalOn outperforms the evaluated baselines on most benchmarks. It leads all reported relation extraction benchmarks and achieves the highest average F1 for event triggers and arguments with gold triggers. The same model also performs strongly on aspect sentiment triplet extraction and pronoun resolution through its span-pair formulation. A correction for the probability bias introduced during training improves confidence estimates for entities, relations, and event arguments after calibration, with little change in F1.
  </details>

- **[A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16837)**  `arXiv:2610.16837`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Pengcheng Wang, Zhexuan Zhang, Chao Lou, Kewei Tu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations---one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks---at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[SuPER-Mamba: Surprisal Prioritization for Extended-Context Routing in Mamba](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16636)**  `arXiv:2610.16636`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Zhetong Zhang, Gayan K Kulatilleke_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>

The results show that SuPER-Mamba improves the average score from 8.06 to 15.69, corresponding to a 94.7% relative gain over the Base Models and a 13.1% improvement over the state-of-the-art prior baseline. Ablation and length-wise analyses further support the effectiveness of the proposed routing framework.
  </details>

- **[MixLID: Token-Level Language Identification in Mixed-Language Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16601)**  `arXiv:2610.16601`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Seongtae Hong, Youngjoon Jang, Seungyoon Lee, Jungseob Lee, Heuiseok Lim_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Processing multilingual text requires both identifying a broad range of languages and distinguishing the language of each token in inputs containing multiple languages. We introduce MixLID, a token-level language identification model supporting 111 language-script combinations. MixLID follows a two-stage training process: it first learns to distinguish individual languages using the language labels of monolingual examples, then continues training on mixed-language data. The second stage uses concatenated examples from existing code-switching data alongside augmented examples created through word substitution based on correspondences between English source words and loanwords. For monolingual identification, MixLID outperforms all baselines in both accuracy and macro F1 on four benchmarks within the language coverage shared with each baseline. For mixed-language identification, it outperforms the baselines in identifying the language of individual tokens on every evaluated language pair. MixLID achieves high performance across a broad range of languages in both monolingual and mixed-language settings. The model is publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[PatTransBench: an ipc-stratified, multi-dimensional benchmark for patent machine translation evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16538)**  `arXiv:2610.16538`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Xiaowei Su, Xusen Cheng_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present PatTransBench, a 12,000-item Chinese-English/Japanese/Korean patent machine translation (PatMT) benchmark with a four-dimensional evaluation protocol. The benchmark comprises 6,000 short-text (sentence/claim) and 6,000 long-text (paragraph) pairs, evenly split across three language pairs and both translation directions, built via IPC-section-stratified sampling and dualthreshold quality gating from upstream patent-family parallel corpora.   </details>

- **[Avoiding What Your Teacher Already Knows: Entity Familiarity for Deep-Search Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16251)**  `arXiv:2610.16251`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Yifei Liu, Zhixiang Liang, Wentao Tan, Yicheng Wang, Jiaqi Wang, Nan Duan, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deep-search agents are commonly trained by distilling tool-use trajectories from stronger teacher models. However, structurally complex questions may remain relatively easy for teachers familiar with key entities in the underlying entity graph, resulting in lower search demand and weaker supervision. We refer to this teacher-specific variation in question difficulty as teacher-relative difficulty and investigate entity familiarity as an early predictor. We first introduce Evidence-Verified Entity Familiarity (EVF), which estimates familiarity by verifying a teacher-generated factual brief against online evidence. Across multiple teachers, EVF is significantly correlated with teacher-relative difficulty with AUCs of 0.60--0.70. However, its high cost makes it impractical for constructing entity graphs at scale. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Reported Entity Familiarity (SEF), a lightweight gating signal that directly asks a teacher whether it is familiar with an entity before admitting that entity into the graph. Across multiple teachers, trajectories from SEF-gated synthesis exhibit greater observed search demand and yield higher downstream student accuracy than those from ungated synthesis. Because familiarity is teacher specific, we further study cross-teacher reuse. We screen graphs collected for other teachers using Kimi-K3's SEF judgments and use the retained graphs to produce 5,411 additional trajectories. Combined with 2,200 trajectories from newly constructed, SEF-gated graphs, these data improve Qwen3.8-27B's accuracy from 44.10% to 66.41% on a BrowseComp subset, and achieving state-of-the-art performance among models of comparable size on BrowseComp, SEAL-0, HLE-text, and xbench. Overall, SEF provides a low-cost way to synthesize more informative supervision for deep-search distillation.
  </details>

- **[Query Your Way Out: Benchmarking Multi-Turn Knowledge Reasoning through Generalized Puzzle Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16133)**  `arXiv:2610.16133`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Xin Cheng, Junming Yang, Ning Xu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Puzzles offer a natural testbed for Large Language Models (LLMs) reasoning because they pose verifiable goals under partial information and require multi-step decisions to reach a solution. However, existing puzzle benchmarks typically focus on narrow environments with rigid mechanics and tightly constrained solution targets. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Active Probing Benchmark (APB), which generalizes puzzle-solving by casting concept identification as an interactive reasoning task that integrates specialized knowledge assessment into the puzzle setting. Specifically, APB evaluates whether models can acquire information via multi-turn active probing and inference to pinpoint 960 target concepts of specialized difficulty across eight diverse academic domains. Our evaluation reveals a counter-intuitive phenomenon: most open-source reasoning models significantly underperform their standard instruction counterparts. This finding suggests that in interactive settings, these models struggle to leverage procedural reasoning to reliably access and apply specialized domain knowledge. Beyond these empirical insights, APB provides a scalable pipeline for generating benchmarks that probe knowledge reasoning under interaction across diverse settings.
  </details>

- **[Of Errors and Echoes: Responsibility-Aware Credit Assignment for Tool-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16027)**  `arXiv:2610.16027`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Xingjian Diao, Tianyu Yang, Wenjun Huang, Xiangchi Yuan, Chunhui Zhang, Xingchen Zhao, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning improves tool-use agents, yet fine-grained credit assignment remains challenging even with step-level feedback. An observed error may be inherited from an earlier decision, while multiple responsible decisions may share the same downstream consequence or participate in later recovery. We introduce Error-Chain-Aware Optimization (ECHO), a responsibility-aware credit assignment framework that separates responsibility identification from credit allocation. A frozen judge combines retrospective trajectory analysis with decision-time assessment from the policy-visible prefix to distinguish newly introduced errors, inherited consequences, missed corrections, and successful corrections. ECHO then counts shared downstream consequences once across responsible decisions and constrains rewards for repairing self-induced errors through source-funded recovery, producing bounded action-level supervision alongside terminal supervision. Experiments on six diverse tool-use benchmarks at both 4B and 8B scales show strong and consistent improvements over the compared baselines, with ECHO achieving the highest score on five of six benchmarks at each scale. These results support decision responsibility as a useful basis for fine-grained credit assignment in tool-use agents. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[An Explainable System for Offensive Content Detection in Nastaliq Urdu: Corpus Curation, Transformer Benchmarking, and Word-Level Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15795)**  `arXiv:2610.15795`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Muhammad Shahid Iqbal Malik_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Automated moderation systems are deployed at scale, yet they remain opaque to the users and moderators affected by their decisions, and their coverage is almost entirely confined to English. For Urdu written in the Nastaliq script, no such system exists, and the annotated resources it would be built on are drawn largely from Twitter/X, where character limits constrain how users write. Interpretability has received little attention, leaving it unclear what such models actually learn. This study addresses these gaps in three steps. First, we curate and publicly release a corpus of 7604 Nastaliq Urdu Facebook comments, extending an earlier corpus by correcting text-level inconsistencies and re-examining the original labels. Second, we fine-tune four Urdu-capable transformers under a common grid-search protocol and compare them against twelve feature-classifier baselines on identical data partitions. The best configuration, Multilingual Representations for Indian Languages (MuRIL), reaches 87.05% accuracy and 87.06% macro F1, improving on the strongest baseline by 5.52 percentage points, a margin that exceeds the 95% confidence interval on test accuracy; the two leading transformers differ by less than the test set can resolve, and performance is stable across five optimizers. Third, we compute word-level SHAP attributions adapted to right-to-left rendering. Attribution mass concentrates on high-frequency slurs but extends to syntactically neutral function words and to political vocabulary characteristic of the source pages, indicating that aggregate performance may rest partly on lexical and topical regularities rather than a generalizable representation of offensiveness.
  </details>

- **[In-Place Indic Tokenizer Expansion and Continual Pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15373)**  `arXiv:2610.15373`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Avinash Benki, Prasanjith Pasunuti, Sutanshu Saksena Raj, Parijat Chatterjee, Nayanjit Sarkar, Daksh Maan_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We adapted Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B for eight Indian languages without changing its backbone architecture. We expanded the vocabulary in place from 131,072 to 163,072 entries using continued byte-pair encoding and AdaptMix rebalancing, reducing tokens per word by 38.6%. We initialized new input and output rows by averaging their original constituent rows, then trained them on 90% Indic and 10% English text before updating the backbone. Continual pretraining then progressed through broad training, high-quality annealing, and long-context training over approximately 1.27 trillion tokens. The annealed checkpoint gained 12.9 points on the Indic MILU benchmark but lost 3.4 on English MMLU. We also report practical negative results. Direct token addition underperformed continued byte-pair encoding. AdamW weight decay changed rows intended to stay fixed. Perplexity on an Indic-heavy holdout did not select the learning rate that best preserved English performance.
  </details>

- **[A Sovereign, Indic-First, Reasoning Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15371)**  `arXiv:2610.15371`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Sutanshu Saksena Raj, Prasanjith Pasunuti, Parijat Chatterjee, Daksh Maan, Purusharth Malik, Nayanjit Sarkar, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Gnani-Evon-v3.3-30B-A3B is a long-context hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model for reasoning, instruction following, and tool use in English and eight Indian languages. Starting from NVIDIA's Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B checkpoint, it retains the 52-layer backbone and changes the vocabulary, training data, and post-training objectives. An in-place expansion from 131,072 to 163,072 tokens reduces mean Indian-language fertility by 38.6%. The new embedding rows are initialized from their upstream decompositions and warmed before the backbone is updated. Continual pretraining then adds broad English-Indic data, high-quality annealing, and direct training at a 131,072-token sequence length.The central result appears after post-training. Reinforcement learning across four verifiable task environments improves mathematics, graduate-level science, and instruction following, but degrades Indic extractive question answering because the rewards do not require an answer in the requested language. The share of Indic extraction items answered in English rises from 8.7% to 91.7%. Accuracy conditional on answering in the target script roughly doubles, which is consistent with preserved reading ability but is measured on a self-selected subset.Two unreleased studies test repairs. A scoped Indic reward restores the language convention. A 26B-A4B generative judge outperforms a 235B-parameter model on RM-Bench, and distillation restores 81% of the capabilities displaced by optimizing against it.Relative to the architecture-identical starting checkpoint, the released model gains 5.2 points on an Indic aggregate while giving up 1.7 points of English retention. The unreleased Indic-aware branch trades further, gaining 14.6 Indic points at a cost of 5.4 in English. A planned FP8 release reduces the artifact to 32GB with near-zero mean change across 32 paired benchmarks.
  </details>

- **[North or South? Diagnosing LLMs' Understanding of North Korean Language, Society, and Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15282)**  `arXiv:2610.15282`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Kiwoong Park, Seyoung Song, Donghyun Woo, Alice Oh_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in multilingual question answering, yet their ability to understand low-resource sociolinguistic contexts remains under-explored. We study North Korea as a unique testbed where decades of division have produced distinct differences from South Korea in vocabulary, orthography, norms, and ideological discourse. We introduce LENS (Language and sociocultural Evaluation for North Korean Society), a human-validated benchmark of 1,765 questions evaluating LLMs across three dimensions: linguistic robustness, sociocultural perspective alignment, and domain-specific knowledge. Evaluating diverse recent LLMs, we find a modest performance drop on North Korean language inputs, a larger gap in sociocultural perspective alignment, and severe limitations on domain-specific knowledge. Qualitative analysis reveals that models often conflate formal institutions with lived realities, project liberal-democratic assumptions, or rely on coarse stereotypes. Our results demonstrate that linguistic similarity alone does not guarantee sociocultural or domain-specific understanding, highlighting the critical need for grounded evaluation resources for underrepresented cultural and political contexts.
  </details>

- **[UDHRBench: Benchmarking Human Rights in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15179)**  `arXiv:2610.15179`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Alak Raad, Noreldin Morssy, Zeerak Suhail, Serin Atiani, Mustafa Jarrar_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
