To enable autonomous delegation without additional models at inference time, we introduce a step-level RL method that jointly optimizes task solving and delegation, with fine-grained credit assignment for individual delegation decisions. We also introduce an external judge-based delegation strategy and use it to systematically investigate key design choices in edge-cloud collaboration, including when to delegate, how delegation decisions should be made, what context should be shared, and how frequently the cloud LLM should be invoked. Experiments show that EdgeWise matches or outperforms pure-LLM execution while reducing inference cost up to 62% on SWE-Rebench and 34% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. We further deploy EdgeWise on a local workstation, demonstrating comparable cost savings in a practical edge-cloud setting.
  </details>

- **[UMCR: Universal Medical Concept Recognition through Guideline Integration and Agentic Linking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17363)**  `arXiv:2610.17363`  `cs.CL`  
  _Fabrice Lamarche, Amal Zouaq_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Medical Concept Recognition is the task of extracting and grounding spans in medical text to entries in a standard ontology. Current methods are generally developed towards a single ontology and source text type (clinical notes, drug labels, etc.) The central challenge is therefore to build methods that adapt to any target ontology without requiring ontology-specific retraining. More recent approaches like REAL and AutoPCR make direct use of Large Language Models and can theoretically adapt to any ontology choice but suffer from a lack of generalization. We propose UMCR, a pipeline that allows extraction and linking to any target ontology using any source text variety, utilizing direct guideline integration and an agentic linking module. We evaluate our method on the recent MedPath benchmark, covering a wide variety of medical text types and vocabularies, and show that our method achieves strong performance across these tasks. This ability unlocks interoperability in the healthcare domain, allowing for extraction and alignment between different medical standards. Our method also reduces dependence on parametric LLM memory, thanks to improved interaction with the target ontology compared to other proposed approaches.
  </details>

- **[From Sampled Evidence to Radiology Reports: Objectives, Constraints, and Realization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17318)**  `arXiv:2610.17318`  `cs.CL`  
  _Kun Zhao, Haoteng Tang, Chenghua Lin, Liang Zhan_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Sampling multiple reports creates an inference problem: how should sampled evidence be converted into a final decision, and does a better structured decision yield a better report? We study these questions through a framework that separates the decision signal, scoring objective, and feasible decision set, followed by text realization. On MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, controlled comparisons across 13 generator configurations per benchmark under grouped development/test evaluation reveal three findings. First, changing the objective under fixed evidence and rule capacity changes predictions and their held-out metric trade-offs. Second, relaxing candidate constraints has objective-dependent effects under shared signals and frozen scores. Diagnostics connect the IU macro-oriented assertion increase to near-zero label thresholds and show that limited candidate coverage coexists with selection headroom. Third, a controlled realization study with SFT-Qwen3-VL-8B shows that decision-level gains can be attenuated, amplified, or reversed. Change decomposition reveals that realization can remove incorrect assertions while losing correct findings, so target fidelity and reference accuracy need not improve together. Finding gains also do not consistently improve reference-based report quality. These results motivate separate evaluation of decision rules, candidate constraints, and realized reports.
  </details>

- **[Nufo: A Benchmark for Ewe Automatic Speech Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17278)**  `arXiv:2610.17278`  `cs.CL`  
  _Christ Kekeli Keli, Steve Sanogo, Patrice Sebastiano, Hamad Aldenawi, Ryan Whetten_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Automatic speech recognition (ASR) remains challenging for low-resource languages, where the scarcity of transcribed speech limits the development of accurate systems. This challenge is particularly acute for African languages such as Ewe, which has millions of speakers but remains underrepresented in publicly available ASR resources and benchmarks. In this work, we consolidate, normalize, and partition existing Ewe speech resources into a standardized 174-hour Ewe ASR benchmark, the largest to date to our knowledge. We fine-tune and evaluate pretrained speech models, including Whisper and AfriHuBERT, to establish strong baselines on our benchmark. Whisper-medium achieves a word error rate (WER) of 37.98%, while AfriHuBERT achieves 39.70% on the test set. We further provide a qualitative analysis of common recognition errors. We release the benchmark under the name Nufo, derived from the Ewe word for "talk", accompanied by models and evaluation resources, to facilitate future research on Ewe and other underrepresented African languages.
  </details>

- **[DuoDiscover: Scaling Autonomous Discovery Beyond the Evaluation Bottleneck](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17184)**  `arXiv:2610.17184`  `cs.CL`  
  _Shubham Agarwal, Akshat Gupta, Mike Heddes, Dilara Soylu, Rui Meng, Patrick Tser Jern Kon, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Evaluation has been central to advances in AI, and it is equally critical to autonomous discovery. Yet scaling autonomous discovery to real-world engineering challenges faces a fundamental bottleneck: the cost of evaluating progress. In real settings, a single true evaluation, such as a full benchmark or serving trace, can take hours, so a search can afford only a handful of true evaluations. We present DuoDiscover, a search system that jointly discovers what to optimize and how to evaluate progress efficiently, through three mechanisms. First, each worker in a fleet of coding agents co-discovers an optimization target and a fast, tailored proxy evaluator, which we call a yardstick. The agent then hill-climbs the yardstick rather than the true evaluation. Second, since search can exploit gaps between a yardstick and the true objective, fidelity tests continually recheck each yardstick's ranking and invalidate any that drift. Third, the fleet is bottom-up, with no central decomposition of the problem. A lightweight orchestrator spawns and terminates agents, briefs running ones, and seeds new agents with others' confirmed work. DuoDiscover enables autonomous optimization from software to chip architecture. We demonstrate DuoDiscover on two repository-level benchmarks and four GPU and TPU kernel suites covering hundreds of kernels. On SWE-fficiency, it doubles the average speedup of human experts. On SOL-Exec, it ranks first on 121 of 235 kernels and in the top three on 212. On the heavily optimized vLLM and SQLite engines, DuoDiscover achieves 1.92$\times$ and 1.38$\times$ gains over the base code. On a CPU microarchitecture optimization task with evaluations of up to 28 hours, DuoDiscover surpasses both AlphaEvolve-based ArchAgent v2 and the best human design, with 1.65$\times$ ArchAgent v2's gain in 16.7 days versus more than 40 days, advancing the frontier of autonomous chip design.
  </details>

- **[ToolHACE: A Dataset for Detecting Hallucinations in Tool-Based LLM Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17125)**  `arXiv:2610.17125`  `cs.CL`  
  _Nikolay Ivanov, Sergey Pletenev, Elisei Rykov, Anatolii Frolov, Bogdan Monogov, Alexander Potekhin, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Tool-augmented language models ground their responses in external tool outputs, improving reliability beyond parametric knowledge alone. However, even when the correct tool is called and returns accurate information, models may still contradict such outputs, omit critical details, or generate unsupported claims. Existing hallucination benchmarks for tool-augmented dialogue primarily focus on the tool-calling stage, evaluating whether the correct tool and arguments are selected, while overlooking errors that arise during post-tool response generation. To address this gap, we introduce ToolHACE, a span-level benchmark for hallucination detection in tool-augmented LLM responses, covering five fine-grained hallucination categories. Through extensive experiments with modern hallucination detectors, we show that post-tool-call hallucinations are widespread and remain challenging to detect. Our results further demonstrate that effective detection requires training on specialized tool-augmented corpora, while transfer from tool-agnostic hallucination datasets performs poorly in this setting. These findings highlight the need for dedicated benchmarks and models for reliable hallucination detection in tool-augmented language systems.
  </details>

- **[AD4EDU: Benchmarking University Lecture Audio Description across Accessibility Standards, Metrics, and Learner Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17042)**  `arXiv:2610.17042`  `cs.CL`  
  _Psychias Stylianos, Gao Yingqiang_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Audio description (AD) aims to enhance the accessibility of visual media for blind and low-vision (BLV) persons. However, in higher education, where slide-based lectures are a default mode of teaching, lecture AD remains largely underexplored. The main reason is that existing production guidelines, evaluation metrics, and benchmark datasets are oriented toward entertainment content and do not transfer to lectures, where ADs must complement the lecturer's speech, resolve deictic references, and fit within narrow pauses. In this work, we propose AD4Edu, consisting of an AD benchmark, AD4Edu-Bench, and a rule-diagnosable evaluation metric, AD4Edu-Eval, for generating and evaluating ADs in higher education. Specifically, we consolidated established accessibility guidance, including WCAG 2.2, the DCMP Description Key, and NCAM's STEM description practices. We further collected silver reference ADs, judge-ordered preference pairs, and pairwise preferences from four BLV raters, and post-trained models with direct preference optimization (DPO) for detailed analysis. Our findings indicate that while the metric reliably detects violations of the standard, ADs that comply with it do not necessarily fulfill the subjective preferences of BLV persons, most notably on description length, underscoring the necessity of active participation of BLV persons in co-designing inclusive AI solutions.
  </details>

- **[Estimating Uncertainty of Omnimodal Large Language Models via External Omnimodal Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16933)**  `arXiv:2610.16933`  `cs.CL`  
  _Iacopo Ghinassi, Hy Nguyen Gia La, Luke Ong_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent work has investigated Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs), models which can take multiple modalities and their combinations as input, as a way forward to have systems really capable of interacting with their environment. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for OLLMs, however, remains an open problem: existing methods largely target at most two modalities at a time, require access to model internals, or re-invocation of the evaluated model. We propose a model-agnostic UQ framework that scores a Chain-of-Thought response entirely through external omni-modal embeddings, measuring the grounding of the reasoning in the multimodal input and its internal coherence. Our contribution is the family of signals and an empirical characterisation of when it is reliable, rather than any single estimator: we find the geometric scores to be largely redundant with one another (mean within-split rank correlation 0.91-0.94) but strongly complementary to answer-dispersion baselines, and their reliability to depend on the generator and the modality. The resulting confidence estimates require no access to logits, hidden states or gradients of the evaluated model and no additional inference from it; they do require segmenting the reasoning trace with an auxiliary model and, for the aggregated score, a labelled calibration set that we show can be as small as 25 examples (although we also show that such a set buys little over fixing one signal a priori). On UNO-Bench, with both a closed and an open model, our scores yield small gains over self-consistency (systematic with the closed generator, mixed with the open one) and are competitive with self-verbalisation and internal-state baselines, especially in open-ended, omni-modal questions where previous state-of-the-art baselines struggle.
  </details>

- **[ANCHOR: Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16859)**  `arXiv:2610.16859`  `cs.CL`  
  _Wenqiang Zhu, Xinping Lei, Zhiyi Lai, Zhengshuo Gong, Tianzhuang He, Songwei Yu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  For repository-grounded coding agents, a functionally correct patch is not necessarily an acceptable one: developers also constrain how the task must be carried out-modification scope, workflow order, validation, tool use, and reporting. This capability, which we call engineering constraint following, remains largely invisible to current evaluations. We introduce ANCHOR (Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding), a benchmark built on naturalistic, multilingual repository tasks spanning eight language groups. ANCHOR combines (i) a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 categories and 78 leaf types distilled from real developer interactions, (ii) an automated pipeline that instantiates task-grounded atomic constraints and composes them into typed AND/THEN/PRIORITY relations, and (iii) a trajectory-grounded evaluation framework that checks both the code diff and the execution trajectory with rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 agent configurations spanning 2 scaffolds and 10 foundation models on 358 tasks, the strongest measured system, Claude Opus 4.8 under Cline, reaches 70.1% atomic compliance and 63.7% relation compliance, while 19.0% of tasks pass every scored checklist item under the strict all-item FCCR criterion. A five-engineer audit of constraints from 50 instances reports 94% feasibility, 94% repository consistency, and 96% realism. In the primary paired set (14 configurations), the mean signed change in task completion after adding constraints is +0.7 percentage points; individual changes vary in both directions. These results distinguish functional success from constraint compliance, with failures concentrated in workflow ordering, tool-use discipline, and reporting, and substantial interactions between models and scaffolds.
  </details>

- **[The Multilingual Artificial Hivemind: Do All LLMs Think Alike in Every Language?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16755)**  `arXiv:2610.16755`  `cs.CL`  
  _Xaver Raphael Davey, Shubhra Mishra, Anton Adelöw, Siyao Liu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Text generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) often remains limited in diversity compared to that produced by humans. Recent advances demonstrate the presence of inter- and intra-model collapse in open-ended generation of English text, raising concerns about the long-term homogenization of LLM, and more importantly, human thought. However, our understanding of whether this homogenization extends to languages beyond English is limited. In this work, we investigate the role of language on output diversity. Specifically, we aim to understand whether multilingual LLM-generated text is also homogeneous, and whether this homogeneity matches what we observe in humans. Across 23 open-weight models and 13 languages, we find that the artificial hivemind effect is pervasive but uneven in its extent. The intra-model effect holds in three different embedding spaces and under a lexical metric that uses no embedding model, so it is not an artifact of how diversity is measured. The size of the homogenization gap is associated with a model's competence in a language, measured on a held-out translation benchmark, robustly across embedding spaces. Thus, we demonstrate a performance-diversity tradeoff in multilingual LLMs.
  </details>

- **[Support or Magnitude? Characterizing Neuron Relevance for Instruction Data Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16531)**  `arXiv:2610.16531`  `cs.CL`  
  _Yifan Le_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Model-internal signals, such as neuron activations and gradients, have been used for instruction data selection, yet how neuron relevance should be characterized remains underexplored. In particular, should selection prioritize the magnitude of relevance or how broadly it is distributed across neurons? To investigate this question, we construct sample-level relevance profiles using AttnLRP-guided attribution and introduce two complementary criteria: Effective Relevance Support (ERS), which measures the effective support of positive relevance, and Positive Relevance Magnitude (PRM), which captures its average strength. Our analyses reveal that these characterizations produce distinct sample rankings and selection preferences despite sharing the same underlying relevance profiles. On Qwen2 models, PRM exhibits stronger associations with activation-based selection, whereas ERS produces substantially different rankings. These differences extend to task composition, within-task sample preferences, and semantic selection patterns, with varying degrees of agreement across backbones. Experiments across three language models and five downstream benchmarks demonstrate the practical value of relevance-guided selection, with ERS achieving the best overall average performance rank among the evaluated methods. Our findings highlight that how neuron relevance is distributed and characterized, rather than its magnitude alone, matters for instruction data selection.
  </details>

- **[CivWorldBench: Evaluating Language World Models in Structured Multi-Agent Sandbox Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16450)**  `arXiv:2610.16450`  `cs.CL`  
  _Ang Li, Haofei Yu, Zhengwei Tao, Liang Chen, Kuan Li, Miaomiao Li, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The growing use of language models for forecasting motivates a broader evaluation of their world-model capabilities. Such evaluation must go beyond predictive accuracy to assess hidden-state inference and intervention prediction. Real-world forecasting benchmarks offer limited access to hidden-state ground truth and controlled experiments. We introduce CivWorldBench, a benchmark built on a multi-agent strategy game engine with recorded internal states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts. Its 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds support three task levels: association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction. Reference predictors support attributable evaluation of capability gaps, with an expert harness and empirical ceiling estimates contextualizing scores. Stored trajectories make intermediate predictions verifiable, while agent-play experiments test whether world-model capabilities support decision-making. The main panel comprises eleven frontier language models. Composite benchmark scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels, more closely than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a proxy for real-world forecasting capability. Strong association forecasts do not consistently extend to belief inference or intervention prediction, and effect magnitudes remain poorly calibrated despite informative direction predictions. Process verification reveals errors missed by final-answer evaluation, and structured reasoning improves intervention prediction for the strongest model in the process study. Agent-play experiments identify useful assisted plans and motivate evaluating decision-relevant capabilities beyond association forecasting. These findings identify hidden-state inference, intermediate-state prediction, and effect calibration as priorities for world-model training.
  </details>

- **[PersonaFactor: Preference Factors with Dynamic Selection for LLM Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16372)**  `arXiv:2610.16372`  `cs.CL`  
  _Hang Su, Zequn Liu, Jianghan Chao, Qiuyu Tian, Xuesong Lu, Yingce Xia_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Although users may express different personalization needs across tasks, these task-specific behaviors can reflect shared underlying preference mechanisms. Existing LLM personalization methods often focus on surface-level interactions or undifferentiated histories, overlooking the shared mechanisms underlying these behaviors. We introduce PersonaFactors, a framework that distills reusable and interpretable personalization factors from heterogeneous user interactions. We construct a library of thirteen PersonaFactors by extracting evidence-grounded rationales and clustering recurring patterns across tasks, and develop a dynamic factor-guided generation framework that selects factors relevant to each user's history and current request. Across four personalization benchmarks and four backbone models, Dynamic PersonaFactor achieves the best score on every reported metric. Representation analyses further show that PersonaFactors and user history induce partially overlapping low-dimensional representations, and that their joint use yields complementary shifts. Taken together, these findings suggest that factor-based and history-based personalization can mutually reinforce each other.
  </details>

- **[Rule vs.Consequence: Dissociable Internal Representations of Moral Reasoning in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16371)**  `arXiv:2610.16371`  `cs.CL`  
  _Eugenie Shi_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models are increasingly deployed in morally and legally sensitive contexts, yet little is known about how they internally represent distinctions between moral reasoning styles. We ask whether a model's differential response to rule-framed and consequence-framed moral questions reflects distinct internal structure or merely surface lexical sensitivity. We construct a 2$\times$2 factorial dataset crossing reasoning style (rule-based vs. consequence-based framing) with judgment polarity (permissive vs. prohibitive), drawn from three established moral reasoning benchmarks and evaluated on a cleanroom test set of novel phrasings that includes conflict pairs where the two framings predict opposite labels. Using linear probing and activation steering, we identify two orthogonal directions in the residual stream: Dir-A tracks reasoning style and Dir-B tracks judgment polarity, each near-blind to the other factor (cross-correlation $|r| < 0.04$). This double dissociation replicates across three instruction-tuned models from different developers at comparable proportional depth, and it is not knife-edged in layer: the directions are recoverable and causally effective throughout an extended band of the network. Dir-A can causally change judgments, and in conflicting scenarios, it selectively corrects errors in rule-based judgments without changing consequence-based judgments, suggesting that it does not simply make the model more likely to accept everything. Generalization beyond the training templates is partial: the direction transfers across benchmark sources, but its advantage over lexical baselines on novel phrasings is modest. We therefore frame the result as moral reasoning style sensitivity, a geometrically dissociable and causally effective structure, rather than internalized normative reasoning.
  </details>

- **[Strong yet Controllable LLM Abstention without Learning to Abstain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16318)**  `arXiv:2610.16318`  `cs.CL`  
  _Junwei Zhang, Yifei Wang, Wanli Yang, Hexiang Tan, Rui Tang, Xin Chen, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) can reduce hallucination by abstaining from questions they would likely get wrong. Abstention can be implemented outside the model (selective answering) using a confidence threshold that controls the answer rate (coverage), or learned inside it (abstention training), which can perform better but fixes coverage once trained. To compare the two, we match their coverage and decompose risk (error rate) into answering ability and distinguishing ability, i.e., how well the model answers and how accurately it abstains, respectively. The decomposition shows that abstention training performs better mainly by answering better: with strong confidence estimators, the two have nearly equal distinguishing ability. This motivates Train for Accuracy, then Post-hoc Select (TAPS), a modular approach that keeps coverage controllable, needs only standard post-training and an off-the-shelf confidence estimator, and benefits from advances in either component. Across three LLMs and three factual QA benchmarks, TAPS with a probing-based confidence estimator attains 1.5--9.4 percentage points lower mean risk than three representative abstention training methods at matched coverage. Within TAPS, accuracy training often weakens the model's own confidence signals, yet refitting the estimator largely preserves distinguishing ability. Together, these results establish TAPS as a strong yet controllable baseline and raise the bar for future abstention training: sacrificing control over coverage should yield gains beyond what can be achieved by optimizing answering and abstaining separately.
  </details>

- **[More Reasoning Is Not Always Better: Executing Clinical Guidelines with LLMs and Rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15912)**  `arXiv:2610.15912`  `cs.CL`  
  _Xiaoqian Lu, Guangfu Guo, Long Cheng, Kunpeng Liu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in clinical decision support. However, existing approaches often rely on multi-step reasoning or multi-agent collaboration to execute clinical guidelines, introducing substantial computational overhead without reliably preventing decision errors. To address these limitations, we propose a framework for Medical Decision Execution (MedDEx) that integrates structured patient states with deterministic rule execution to support guideline-based treatment planning. MedDEx separates clinical record interpretation from guideline execution, leveraging LLMs to extract patient information and generate treatment plans while assigning guideline-defined decision logic to a rule executor. Experiments across multiple clinical guideline benchmarks demonstrate that MedDEx improves decision accuracy while reducing inference costs. Further analyses highlight the critical roles of structured patient representations and deterministic rule execution, suggesting that additional LLM reasoning does not necessarily translate into better guideline adherence.
  </details>

- **[RIVO: Lightweight Adaptive Rerouting for Deep Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15910)**  `arXiv:2610.15910`  `cs.CL`  
  _Mingchen Li, Jiatan Huang, Hong Yu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deep Research agents rely on long-horizon reasoning and iterative tool use to solve complex information-seeking tasks. However, adaptive decision-making over these trajectories remains challenging, as agents may stop prematurely when further evidence is needed, continue unnecessarily after sufficient evidence has been gathered, or fail to redirect unproductive trajectories. Existing solutions either require costly model retraining and dense turn-level supervision, or rely on heuristic control rules that are not directly optimized for downstream research utility. This motivates a lightweight, utility-aware alternative for Deep Research control. We formulate adaptive rerouting in long-horizon Deep Research as a state-conditioned trajectory correction problem. Based on this view, we introduce RIVO, a lightweight plug-in framework for adaptive trajectory correction. The agent estimates its research state from lightweight signals and determines whether trajectory redirection is needed. Once triggered, the plug-in modifies the Host token logits to steer generation toward a more promising research direction. Theoretical analysis shows that, under a value-alignment condition and bounded local curvature, a sufficiently small logit intervention can locally improve expected downstream research utility. We further construct BrowseCore, a curated dataset with a paired local corpus, for efficient and controlled Deep Research experimentation. Building on this resource, the plug-in is trained from downstream outcomes, enabling it to learn corrections that improve subsequent research and final task performance. Extensive experiments across multiple Deep Research benchmarks and control settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, showing that lightweight logit intervention can improve long-horizon research without retraining the underlying Host model.
  </details>

- **[NepPlural: A Human-Anchored Benchmark for Persona Annotation in Nepali Migration Discourse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15732)**  `arXiv:2610.15732`  `cs.CL`  
  _Jinu Nyachhyon, Anish Khatiwada, Bimal Timilsina_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Pluralistic alignment asks that language models faithfully represent a society's diverse, competing values rather than collapse them into one dominant viewpoint, yet flagship pluralistic-alignment datasets remain heavily skewed toward Western respondents. We introduce NepPlural, a human-anchored benchmark for modelling competing socio-cultural personas in Nepali public discourse on youth migration and brain drain. We curate 2,148 code-mixed (Devanagari, Romanized Nepali, English) YouTube comments, annotate them along a four-axis persona taxonomy (Intent, Primary Driver, Value Orientation, Affect) plus an explicit No-Persona class, and build a 300-comment gold set labelled independently by three native Nepali speakers (mean Fleiss' $\kappa \approx 0.55$). Using this gold set to audit automatic annotation, we find that LLM annotation reliability is driven by protocol. Labels collected in batches through chat interfaces reach only near-chance inter-model agreement ($\kappa \approx 0.17$). Annotating one comment at a time raises agreement above the native-speaker level ($\kappa \approx 0.72$), but consistency is not validity: under a forced-choice schema, models agree on personas for the 39% of comments native speakers judge to express none, keeping macro-F1 against human gold near 0.50. Allowing abstention resolves this: models recover No-Persona comments with F1 of 0.79 to 0.87 and, against leave-one-annotator-out references, match or exceed individual native speakers (macro-F1 0.75 to 0.86 vs. 0.75). Encoders fine-tuned on the batched labels reach only 0.34. Finally, a human-judged steerability probe finds that three frontier models adopt single persona axes with 59 to 77% fidelity but compose full personas only 33% of the time, with no congruence gap detected at this scale between Western-congruent and Nepali-collectivist personas.
  </details>

- **[Rate-Resolved Text Evaluation with Masked Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15667)**  `arXiv:2610.15667`  `cs.CL`  
  _Yiqi Liu, Kun Zhao, Chenghua Lin, Nafise Sadat Moosavi_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A single evaluation score can rank generation systems but rarely reveals what failed. We propose rate-resolved text evaluation, which turns the masking rate of masked diffusion language models into a diagnostic axis. By reconstructing text under different fractions of masked tokens, one diffusion score becomes a vector of band-conditioned scores that reflect reconstruction difficulty at varying levels of visible context. On SummEval, preserving this rate structure yields complementary signal: the best masking-rate band improves fusion with autoregressive likelihood over a collapsed diffusion scalar, survives a sample-shuffle control that breaks rate ordering, and adds residual signal to a fixed prompted judge. A second diffusion model reproduces the effect more weakly. On WMT MQM zh-en, roundtrip mask-and-reconstruct probing produces a tunable localization curve in which ranking-oriented AUROC and span-detection F1 peak at different masking rates. Factuality benchmarks bound the interpretation: band semantics are model- and task-dependent, so each application requires empirical validation.
  </details>

- **[Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15542)**  `arXiv:2610.15542`  `cs.CL`  
  _Project Apertus, Yixuan Xu, Yassine Turki, Vinko Sabolčec, Valentina Pyatkin, Tommy Chu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Language models are becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure built in the open, by public institutions, on documented data, is the alternative to dependence on a few providers; Apertus shows this is viable at scale. Apertus 1.5 extends the fully open Apertus family from text to multimodal reasoning. Continued pretraining of the Apertus 1.0 models, on 4T additional tokens for the 8B and 2T for the 70B, adds image and audio understanding and extends the context window fourfold to 262,144 tokens; multimodality enters through the tokenizer, the language-model head remains restricted to text, and the architecture is unchanged. Supervised finetuning, long-context finetuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and preference alignment complete the released models. Thinking is a flag of the chat template rather than a separate model, and lifts mathematical reasoning by up to 20 points on the 8B model. The released models improve over their predecessors on nearly every benchmark; among fully open models of its class, the 8B leads on knowledge, instruction following, and cultural benchmarks, and its instruction following surpasses all compared models, including open-weight ones. On image and audio understanding, a first for the family, the models are competitive with fully open multimodal models, strongest on document understanding and long-form and lower-resource speech recognition, while specialized vision and audio models remain ahead on perception and transcription of English and other high-resource languages. As in Apertus 1.0, we train only on openly available data, respect crawler opt-outs retroactively, and exclude restrictively licensed material. We release the model weights, data preparation and training recipes, and evaluation suites under permissive licenses; openness extends to values, with the Apertus charter guiding alignment stages published alongside the models.
  </details>

- **[Do correct answers have stable latent knowledge support?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15277)**  `arXiv:2610.15277`  `cs.CL`  
  _Chuancheng Shi, Shangze Li, Wenhua Wu, Kun Hu, Fei Shen, Zhiyong Wang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models are typically evaluated in terms of the correctness of their output. However, output correctness alone does not confirm whether the latent knowledge supporting an answer has stable internal representations. We therefore propose latent state stability (LSS) and knowledge topology stability (KTS) to investigate the stability of individual knowledge states and their relational structure, respectively. Specifically, we first separately average the model's internal representations of the same knowledge under each elicitation condition. Using the mean representation under the baseline condition as a reference, we remove shared shifts to obtain corrected representations. We then formulate LSS as the distance between each corrected representation and its reference representation, normalized against the typical distance between knowledge items of the same type. We formulate KTS as the cross-condition consistency of the ordered pairwise representation distances among knowledge items of the same type. Next, we construct EpiStableBench, which comprises 4,411 items spanning factual knowledge and mathematical reasoning, with 76,766 controlled queries. Across 16 LLMs from four families, representation stability varies substantially even among items answered correctly under the base condition. Within models, higher stability generally corresponds to higher accuracy under held-out elicitation conditions; across models, stability does not consistently increase with model size or overall accuracy. Meanwhile, we present LatentDPO to learn a knowledge-editing policy that accounts for the stability of latent knowledge. Experimental results show that integrating LatentDPO with multiple existing editing methods consistently improves editing success and generalization across different expressions.
  </details>

- **[Lumen-bench: Cross-Lingual Safety Gaps and the Say-Do Problem in Tool-Calling Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15134)**  `arXiv:2610.15134`  `cs.CL`  
  _Giovana Kerche Bonás, Thiago Laitz, Thales Sales Almeida, João Guilherme Alves Santos_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  When a large language model refuses an unethical request, what does refusal mean? In conversation, refusal is bounded by what the model says; once the model is equipped with executable tools, what it does can diverge from what it says, a failure mode that English-only evaluations cannot fully reveal. We introduce Lumen-bench, a behavioral benchmark of tool-calling ethics spanning 30 models, five languages (Portuguese, English, Spanish, Mandarin Chinese, Hindi), 108 Portuguese-authored scenarios, six social-pressure conditions, two system prompts (ethical and neutral), and 21 generic tools. The evaluation comprises 194,400 trials. Judgments come from a reasoning-model judge (o4-mini), calibrated against one Portuguese-speaking author ($n=83$; harmful/non-harmful $\kappa=0.78$), compared with two other provider judges (Fleiss' $\kappa=0.78$, $n=607$), and complemented by retrospective sandbox replay. Four findings emerge. (i) Within-model comparisons support higher harmful-action rates in Hindi and Portuguese than English under the ethical prompt, and Hindi and Spanish under the neutral prompt, after multiple-testing correction. (ii) Premium models have lower median violation rates, although price does not guarantee safety or competence. (iii) Replacing the ethical system prompt with a neutral one raises pooled violation rates from 2.76\% to 13.64\%. (iv) In 8.57\% of substantive-call cases, refusal or ethical objection accompanies a harmful tool call: the judges consistently identify the say-do gap, although they differ in how many responses they assign to this category. Matched benign controls demonstrate legitimate task completion in 82.8\% of 3,300 trials. Code and reproduction scripts are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[RegExtract: A Benchmark for PFAS Regulatory Information Extraction with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15103)**  `arXiv:2610.15103`  `cs.CL`  
  _Defne Circi, Krystelle Lionti, Sarathkrishna Swaminathan, Daniel P. Sanders, L. Catherine Brinson, Bhuwan Dhingra, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Extracting structured information from regulatory documents is a critical but challenging task. Relevant facts are scattered across long, legally dense texts, and traceability of extracted facts to their source is essential for verification. With increasing awareness of the environmental and health impacts of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), regulatory documents have expanded significantly, varying in scope and product relevance, making interpretation challenging for manufacturers and policymakers. We introduce RegExtract, a benchmark for structured information extraction from PFAS regulatory documents, comprising 488 human-annotated field instances across 20 US state documents and 46 regulations. Each field instance includes a value and a provenance entry, yielding 976 entries in total. We define a typed, multi-field schema targeting key elements such as material definitions, permitted uses, and product exemptions, and propose provenance-aware evaluation metrics tailored to regulatory text. Through experiments with open- and closed-source LLMs across prompting strategies, document condensing methods, and schema partitioning approaches, we find that document identification fields remain challenging, and that field-specific few-shot examples improve extraction. This work lays the groundwork for AI tools for hazardous substance identification, question answering, and compliance monitoring. The code and data are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[TeachGrade: Training-Free Short Answer Scoring with Teacher Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14900)**  `arXiv:2610.14900`  `cs.CL`  
  _Jinhao Yan, Zhihong Shen, Shengjie Wang, Yiting Ren, Wentao Zhang, Yilei Wang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-subject, multi-step scoring requires consistent partial credit across grading conventions. We introduce TeachGrade, a training-free framework using teacher-graded examples. The Task Adapt module builds two frozen memories: Skill captures contextual teacher preferences beyond the rubric; CaseBank supplies local evidence. PreJudge provides retrieval cues; FinalJudge regrades the answer without preliminary scores. On 3,829 SAS-Bench answers across 12 tasks, official macro collaborative consistency score (CCS) rises from Native's 67.99 to 81.32 (+13.33 points), and pooled step exact match from 54.85% to 62.71%. Macro quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) reaches 84.71, exceeding Native, OpenJudge, ProofGrader, and Trojsten by 9.52, 3.50, 11.37, and 17.43 points, respectively, and leading on 8 tasks. Local Qwen3.8-27B gains 8.83 CCS and 4.08 QWK points, improving CCS on all 12 tasks. QWK gains over Native span 6.38--14.65 points on Portuguese automatic essay scoring (AES) and 2.16--2.24 on ASAP-SAS across label views, with lower mean absolute error. These results support reuse across languages, response formats, and backbones without weight updates.
  </details>

- **[Social Bias in Chinese Large Language Models under Social Media Expressions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14879)**  `arXiv:2610.14879`  `cs.CL`  
  _Mo Zhou_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Existing Chinese social-bias benchmarks for large language models largely rely on normalized or template-based expressions, leaving the influence of internet slang, emoji, and sarcasm insufficiently examined. Safety alignment may further compress conventional plausibility ratings toward the lower end of the scale. This study constructs 73 paired probes across gender, region, and occupation. Each probe contains a neutral expression, a social-media-style expression, and a reversed-identity control. The task is reframed from direct plausibility judgment to social consensus estimation. Social-media expressions are divided into stylistic packaging, which preserves semantic polarity, and sarcastic packaging, which reverses surface polarity. Six Chinese-capable large language models are evaluated through paired differences measuring identity bias, stylistic packaging, and sarcasm shift. All models show significant identity-bias effects; five show significantly negative stylistic-packaging effects; and sarcasm shifts display a clear cross-model gradient. These findings demonstrate that expression form is not a transparent carrier in bias evaluation and that lower scores under sarcasm should not be interpreted directly as bias mitigation. The proposed paired design offers a measurement approach for Chinese social-media contexts while also revealing the construct boundary and prompt sensitivity of social consensus estimation.
  </details>

- **[Who Receives Respect? A Counterfactual Benchmark for Honorific Allocation Bias in Bengali](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14769)**  `arXiv:2610.14769`  `cs.CL`  
  _Ajwad Abrar, Md Kamrul Hasan, Hasan Mahmud_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Bengali has no grammatical gender, but honorificity is obligatory: every third-person reference must choose ordinary or respectful register. English has no such signal, so the system must choose a level of deference that the source never specified. We use this property to measure how large language models (LLMs) allocate respect in English--Bengali translation. Our evaluation set contains 2{,}016 sentences across 72 occupations. Each appears in seven sentence frames under four pronoun conditions. Masculine and feminine versions differ by one word, forming counterfactual pairs. We report a single Honorific Bias Score (HBS) for each model on a 0--100 scale, covering both the gender and occupation axes. A lower score means that respect is allocated more evenly. For the occupation analysis, we compute each occupation's honorific rate across the seven no-pronoun sentence frames. The standard deviation of these 72 occupation-level rates ranges from 17.2 to 35.5 percentage points across models, showing substantial variation in how honorifics are allocated across occupations. Occupation is associated with 3.2\% to 51.5\% of the variance in register choice, compared with at most 1.2\% for gender. Gender effects are much smaller overall: only two of the nine models show significant directional gender gaps, and they favor opposite genders. HBS ranges from 19.9 to 70.1 across the nine models, showing substantial variation in how evenly the models allocate respect.
  </details>

- **[The Constitution Speaks Nheengatu: An Open MT System and Reproducible Corpus Pipeline for the Amazonian Língua Geral](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14760)**  `arXiv:2610.14760`  `cs.CL`  
  _Fabrício Carraro, Rodolfo Joel Zevallos, Rodrigo Gonçalves de Souza, Caio Henrique Faustino da Silva, John E. Ortega_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Nheengatu (yrl), the Amazonian Língua Geral, has 6--10 thousand speakers and is co-official in São Gabriel da Cachoeira (Brazil), yet remains poorly served by evaluated Portuguese--Nheengatu MT resources. We present the largest parallel corpus assembled for the language (14.5k Portuguese--Nheengatu pairs), anchored by the 2023 official translation of the Brazilian Federal Constitution; the first MT evaluation set built from transcribed spontaneous speech; and, to our knowledge, the first open-weight MT models dedicated to bidirectional Portuguese--Nheengatu translation.Three findings organize the paper. First, translation into Nheengatu on held-out constitutional articles plateaus on development data regardless of training length or model size, and much of the remaining error sits in conventional legal terms that the written sources do not attest consistently; a terminology success rate over a frozen lexicon shows that glossary mechanisms at training time and lexical constraints at decoding each raise term realization, the latter at a cost in repetitive output that chrF++ barely registers. Second, a corpus expansion that adds transcribed conversation raises speech chrF++ by 24--27 points while leaving written domains unchanged, a register gap that written-only benchmarks cannot see. Third, a larger NLLB model helps translation into Portuguese but not into Nheengatu on legal or speech text. For Portuguese-to-Nheengatu translation, our final systems reach 31.7--32.8 chrF++ on article-disjoint constitutional text, 64.1--64.5 on the near-domain set (62.1 after removing items with target-side content overlap), and 45.2--47.5 on speech.
  </details>

- **[Uniform Information Density-Based Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14578)**  `arXiv:2610.14578`  `cs.CL`  
  _Yongyuan Li, Yang Xu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  To enable large language models to generate outputs that align with human preferences, optimization algorithms based on the comparison between chosen and rejected output pairs have been developed and been proven effective. Some recent endeavors have utilized certain linguistically-derived assumptions about the preference pairs to guide the design of more precise optimization directions. However, human preferences are complex and hard to measure by simplistic criteria, and it is important to incorporate broader and more sophisticated insights about preferred vs. not-preferred language. In this study, we adopt a well-established psycholinguistic theory, Uniform Information Density, to develop a novel preference optimization algorithm, UIDPO. The basic assumption is that humans prefer to produce language in which information is uniformly distributed, because uniformity induces less cognitive processing effort. To implement this idea into the algorithm, we derive a compound metric for information uniformity by combining the global standard deviation and the local second-order difference, and integrate it to the objective of preference optimization. We compare UIDPO with SimPO, a previous state-of-the-art method, obtaining comparable and sometimes better performance on AlpacaEval2, ArenaHard, and MT-Bench. Additional linguistic analysis on complement clauses also shows that UIDPO can better reflect the tendencies of keeping information uniform in natural language than baselines. Our results show that the subtle human preference over the information rate in language is a helpful source for achieving better human alignment for LLMs. The code repository is published here:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[LongHisDoc: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chinese Long Historical Document Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14531)**  `arXiv:2610.14531`  `cs.CL`  
  _Zeyu Shan, Yongxin Shi, Shihang Wu, Peirong Zhang, Yuanyuan Fang, Zhaopeng Wang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Chinese historical documents are invaluable cultural treasures, but their complexity poses significant comprehension challenges for non-specialists. Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) in modern document tasks, their capabilities in Long (full-book) Historical Document understanding remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce LongHisDoc, the first benchmark tailored for long historical document understanding. LongHisDoc comprises 1,012 expert-annotated QA pairs derived from 101 PDF documents, with an average of 85.1 pages and 42,776.4 tokens per document. It spans 10 categories and features four QA types: single-page, cross-page, multi-hop, and unanswerable. Answering these questions requires integrating multimodal evidence from text, layout, and visual elements. Our evaluation reveals that the top-performing LVLM and LLM achieve only 62.9% and 69.9% accuracy, respectively, highlighting a substantial performance gap. Furthermore, we assess various modal retrievers and the end-to-end RAG performance to provide references for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. We believe that LongHisDoc serves as a comprehensive benchmark to catalyze future research in full-book historical document understanding. The benchmark and evaluation code are available atthis https URLandthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[SciCurateBench: Curating Experimental Data from Heterogeneous Scientific Literature with Verbal-Action Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14393)**  `arXiv:2610.14393`  `cs.CL`  
  _Minuk Ma, Kaiyun Guo, Jiarui Ding_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open. science/r/scicuratebench-D885/.
  </details>

- **[Evaluating LLMs as Agentic Workflow Executors in Real-World Customer Support Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14346)**  `arXiv:2610.14346`  `cs.CL`  
  _Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar, Gundeep Singh, Xue-Yong Fu, Karol Chang, Kevin Sanders, Shi Zong, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Enterprise customer-support agents increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to execute bounded, tool-using workflows. We study this problem through the lens of Skill LLMs: specialized executors that operate within a selected skill context and must complete a narrow, stateful workflow under policy and tool constraints. We present a benchmark construction pipeline that mines recurrent workflows from real-world transcripts, converts them into structured skill descriptions, maps them to tool requirements, simulates environment state with Model Context Protocol (MCP)-compatible mocks, and generates multi-turn tool-using dialogues. Using this benchmark, we conduct a large-scale zero-shot evaluation of 17 language models spanning closed model families and deployment-oriented open-weight models from 1.7B to 14B parameters, each judged independently by five strong LLM judges, plus a deterministic rule-based evaluator that checks tool coverage, hallucinated tool use, and unsupported claims. We find a consistent ranking in which GPT-5.4 leads by a wide margin and QWEN3.5-9B is the strongest open-weight model (below 20B), outperforming several closed baselines under every judge. We also find that judge choice is not a negligible methodological detail: pairwise judge agreement on the pass/fail verdict averages Kappa=0.524 across 10 judge pairs. These results suggest that comprehensive zero-shot evaluation of skill execution requires judge reliability as carefully as model capability.
  </details>

- **[Latent Core Tokenizer: Compress, but Meaningfully](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12376)**  `arXiv:2610.12376`  `cs.CL`  
  _Felermino D. M. A. Ali, Millicent Ochieng, Ogbemi Ekwejunor-Etchie, Ade Famoti, Jacki O'Neill, Debjit Paul_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Tokenizers are commonly optimized for compression, but a compact vocabulary does not necessarily distribute its capacity evenly across languages. We introduce the Latent Core Tokenizer (LCT), a language-agnostic approach that separates structural discovery from vocabulary construction. LCT uses Minimum Description Length, entropy-based boundary signals, and morphotactic constraints to identify reusable linguistic units before constructing a shared vocabulary. Across 104 languages with a 200K-token vocabulary, LCT achieves lower fertility and higher MorphScore than BPE, Unigram, and parity-aware BPE, while maintaining comparable cross-lingual disparity in tokenization cost. Across four multilingual downstream benchmarks, LCT improves aggregate score by 1.48, 1.83, and 2.00 points over BPE, Unigram, and parity-aware BPE, respectively. Our findings show that compression alone does not predict representation quality and highlight the importance of morphology-driven structural discovery and how frequency is used to allocate the final vocabulary across languages.
  </details>

- **[HarnessSQL: Harness-Native Training for SQL Agents in Realistic Database Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12274)**  `arXiv:2610.12274`  `cs.CL`  
  _Haolin Yang, Jipeng Zhang, Zhiqiang Qian, Jian Xie, Shuaishuai Gong, Sirui Han, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Text-to-SQL models are commonly trained to map questions directly to static queries, whereas real-world database agents operate through stateful, multi-turn interaction with live databases -- inspecting schemas, executing probe queries, diagnosing errors, and revising hypotheses. This creates a critical train-deploy mismatch, as the execution harness that mediates this interaction is introduced only at inference time. To bridge this gap, we propose HarnessSQL, a harness-native post-training framework that preserves the full interaction structure throughout both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. HarnessSQL builds isolated, executable database environments paired with hidden execution oracles, rolls out teachers directly inside the target SQL harness, and retains only verified trajectories for full-sequence SFT, followed by execution-reward RL. Across Spider 2.0-SQLite, HarnessSQL dramatically boosts the execution accuracy of compact models, raising Qwen3-8B from 15.5% to 45.2% and Qwen3-14B from 22.2% to 54.8%, while transferring effectively to out-of-distribution interactive benchmarks such as BIRD-Interact and LiveSQLBench. Our findings demonstrate that training database agents directly within their execution harness is essential for mastering complex, long-horizon database workflows.
  </details>

- **[Nucleus Speculative Decoding: Plausibility-Aware Verification Beyond Exact Distribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07822)**  `arXiv:2610.07822`  `cs.CL`  
  _Shuhao Li, Fanghua Ye, Wanyu Lin, Tianyu Yuan, Xiaoyu Shen_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive generation by letting a lightweight draft model propose tokens that a target model verifies in parallel. However, its standard acceptance rule, designed for exact distribution correction, rejects tokens to which the draft assigns excess probability, even when the target finds them highly plausible: over half of the rejected tokens lie inside the target's own nucleus. Since verification dominates the cost of SD, these rejections waste its most expensive operation. We introduce Nucleus Speculative Decoding (NSD), a plausibility-aware verification rule that accepts a draft token if it passes the standard test or belongs to the target nucleus, while keeping SD's residual correction and bonus sampling unchanged. NSD requires no training or extra forward passes and is compatible with any drafting mechanism. Because it preserves SD's recovery rule, its deviation from the target distribution can be characterized exactly: we prove that the single-step total variation error equals the draft's excess probability inside the target nucleus, which is precisely NSD's gain in acceptance probability. NSD thus trades fidelity for acceptance at an exact one-to-one rate, and we further derive sequence-level fidelity bounds. Across six target models and five mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, NSD achieves the highest throughput among all compared methods, with speedups of up to $5.16\times$ over autoregressive decoding and $3.15\times$ over standard SD, while improving accuracy over SD on five of the six models and nearly halving verification time per output token. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[General Decision Models: Benchmarking and Insights Beyond Jev](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03935)**  `arXiv:2610.03935`  `cs.CL`  
  _Feiyu Duan, Jiayu Lin, Jia Wang, Jun Xiang, Jialiang Wu, Xinnong Zhang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  General decision models, such as Jev, have recently emerged as efficient alternatives to LLMs for structured judgment and selection. But what kinds of decisions can these models reliably make, and how does their behavior change when individual decisions are composed into larger systems? To study this, we introduce JEVal, a bilingual benchmark comprising 11,257 instances from 36 datasets across 10 application domains, and evaluate 25 model configurations spanning general decision models and generative LLMs. Our results show that (1) general decision models are most competitive when decisions can be resolved from available evidence, but weaken when they require specialist knowledge or faithful uncertainty estimation: they can often identify the most likely outcome while substantially overstating its probability. (2) In more dynamic and realistic systems involving long-horizon, multi-step interactions, the advantages of fast local decision making are offset by reliability failures at the system level. on $\tau$-bench, faster local decisions reduce median episode time but lower task success as decision errors accumulate over long trajectories. (3) In large-scale social simulation, decision models approach strong generative LLMs on individual response prediction at substantially lower inference cost, yet remain weaker in user profiling and exhibit larger aggregate estimation errors and systematic bias. Finally, we propose SII-Decision-4B and SII-Decision-27B, which internalize an open-weight LLM's own reasoning into a single-pass first-token decision through Reasoning-to-Readout Self-Distillation, with SII-Decision-27B performing on par with Jev on JEVal while answering a typical query in about 0.1 s.
  </details>

- **[Role-aware Heuristic Episodic Attention for Conversational LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00958)**  `arXiv:2610.00958`  `cs.CL`  
  _Wanyang Hong, Zhaoning Zhang, Yi Chen, Libo Zhang, Baihui Liu, Linbo Qiao, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models often lose track of persistent instructions and relevant information as multi-turn conversations grow. We study this cumulative contextual decay through three related failure modes: attention pollution, dilution, and drift. We propose REA (Role-aware Heuristic Episodic Attention), a context-management framework that assigns different persistence and representation policies to instructions and episodic interactions. Instructional Memory retains identified global constraints in a dedicated prefix. Episodic Memory preserves user inputs and compresses model replies, while heuristic retrieval selects raw text, compressed representations, or omission for each historical turn. On Long-MT-Bench+, REA improves the judge score from 6.32 to 7.36 on a 10-point scale, a 16.5% relative gain over the Vanilla baseline, and reduces average latency by 2.91$\times$. Additional evaluations show aggregate gains on three backbones spanning 1.7B-7B parameters and on Chinese and English role-playing tasks. These results support role-aware context management as a practical approach to maintaining conversational continuity and instruction adherence.
  </details>

- **[Index-Translate: A Multilingual Translation Model Family -- Text, Speech, Controlled Dubbing, and Long-Document Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40181)**  `arXiv:2609.40181`  `cs.CL`  
  _Tianjiao Li, Mengran Yu, Chenyu Shi, Lusheng Zhang, Qisi Chen, Yanshan Zhou, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce Index-Translate, a multilingual translation model family that combines a shared multilingual foundation with specialized training for general translation, instruction following, speech translation, controlled dubbing, and long-document translation. It includes three model sizes, 2B, 9B, and 35B-A3B, and supports translation in 150 languages, with multilingual instruction following. Evaluations on general translation and complex translation instructions show that Index-Translate outperforms translation models of comparable size and achieves performance comparable to 100B-scale translation models and frontier models. Image-text evaluation shows that translation remains possible without image examples in Index-Translate-specific training, although results vary by model size. Index-Echo provides end-to-end speech-to-text and speech-to-speech translation, outperforming existing end-to-end models and achieving performance comparable to frontier omni models. Index-Homura extends the family to syllable-controlled dubbing. Index-NativeLong introduces native long-document translation with a dedicated task formulation and benchmark. These capabilities support diverse translation tasks, including multilingual content production.
  </details>

- **[Gödel Forest: Balancing Search Depth and Breadth for Data-Centric Recursive Self-Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36675)**  `arXiv:2609.36675`  `cs.CL`  
  _Ziqi Zhao, Fanqing Meng, Haocheng Lu, Lingxiao Du, Qiguang Chen, Mengkang Hu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to achieve compounding gains by having models improve themselves. While most existing RSI systems optimize external agent harnesses or prompts around a frozen base model, data-centric RSI directly updates the model's own parameters by training on agent-generated data. However, because validating data strategies requires expensive model training, existing methods face a fundamental dilemma: a single agent gets trapped in narrow directions and lacks exploration breadth, while naive parallel search or heavy trace sharing sacrifices long-horizon search depth. To address this challenge, we introduce G"odel Forest, a multi-agent framework that organizes recursive self-improvement as an ensemble of co-evolving search trees. In G"odel Forest, each agent autonomously grows a persistent tree, deepening, branching, or pruning data strategies based on model feedback to secure depth, while parallel trees explore distinct regions of the data space to expand breadth. Crucially, rather than leaving trees isolated or flooding them with heavy execution logs, a dynamically co-evolving memory connects the forest: agents continuously distill their successes and failures into compact procedural lessons anchored to a global leaderboard. Through this forest ecosystem, a dead-end in one tree instantly warns the whole forest against unpromising paths, while an empirical breakthrough quickly seeds new exploration branches in neighboring trees. Evaluated on RSIBench-Data across six diverse domains, G"odel Forest outperforms the single-agent baseline by an average of 10.70% while reducing wall-clock time on five tasks. Ablations confirm that co-evolving shared memory yields a +7.00% gain over independent parallel search, demonstrating that collective distillation is key to scalable self-improvement. The code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Decision Models vs. LLMs as Rubric Judges: Cheaper, Faster, and Wrong in the Same Places](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29769)**  `arXiv:2609.29769`  `cs.CL`  
  _Delip Rao, Chris Callison-Burch_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM judges now score outputs against rubrics, in benchmarks and as training rewards. Decision models return probabilities over permitted answers with a confidence score but no free text. Two such models are Jev and an open reproduction, Perplexity's Decider. We compare each with three flash-tier LLM judges on nine panels from seven benchmarks with human judgments, giving every judge identical criterion texts. The LLM judges run in two setups, reading a whole rubric at once or one criterion at a time. Our findings suggest both decision models can often stand in for them. The LLM judges cost 16 to 357 times as much and take 5 to 350 times as long, yet in both setups each decision model trails them significantly in at most 6 of 27 comparisons. The two kinds of judge err alike, agreeing more with one another than with the human-annotated judgment labels on ordinal criteria. Over 85% of flash-tier LLM verdicts on either decision model's most confident errors repeat them, where independent errors would give about half. Each decision model's confidence ranks its errors on most ordinal panels, so each is a natural first stage for a cascade deferring uncertain verdicts to an LLM judge. Yet with flash-tier fallbacks, such cascades gained a mere 2.7 points at best over the strongest single judge, even with oracle thresholds, suggesting they mainly save cost. A cascade needs a fallback that is right where its first stage errs, but the LLM judges are mostly wrong in the same places as Jev, and the Decider is already the strongest single judge on most panels. Even each vendor's higher-tier model repeats those errors, and as a fallback it lifted no cascade more than 1.7 points above both tiers' strongest single judge. Holding across setups, effort levels, and tiers, these findings suggest designing future decision models afresh to get right what LLM judges get wrong, and vice versa.
  </details>

- **[Realize What Matters: Principled Context Representation for Large-Scale Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27173)**  `arXiv:2609.27173`  `cs.CL`  
  _Michael Theologitis, Dean Light, Shuyue Stella Li, Benjamin Newman, Yulia Tsvetkov, Dan Suciu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Solving complex tasks in domains such as science, medicine, law, and finance often requires assembling interdependent information scattered across vast, heterogeneous sources far beyond model context limits. Existing approaches tackle this challenge by organizing information into more manageable representations over which models can reason, such as graphs, textual memories, and retrieval collections. These representations dictate what downstream reasoning is possible and, ultimately, whether it succeeds; yet their design and construction remain largely ad hoc. In this work, drawing on the cognitive theory of relevance realization, we propose concrete principles for designing AI systems that construct effective representations of very large contexts. We analyze existing approaches and show how their successes and failures can be explained by their alignment with these principles, and introduce R3Con, a harness that systematically operationalizes them. We evaluate R3Con against nine state-of-the-art baselines on two recent benchmarks of reasoning over large document corpora. On these benchmarks, R3Con substantially outperforms the strongest baseline, by $20$ and $8.4$ percentage points. It also enables smaller models to outperform much larger ones: R3Con with 4B and 9B models outperforms all evaluated 35B baselines, while R3Con with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B outperforms Claude Code with Claude-Sonnet-5 at $3.7\times$ lower cost. Our results show that context representations following our principled approach can reduce reliance on model scale, pointing toward a future of AI systems with frontier-level performance powered by smaller models.
  </details>

- **[From Parameters to Behaviors: A Survey of Model Fusion for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19553)**  `arXiv:2609.19553`  `cs.CL`  
  _Shuo Cai, Yanggan Gu, Zihao Wang, Yuanyi Wang, Yibo Yan, Wenjun Wang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Model fusion integrates the capabilities from source models into a single target model. As of June 2026, Hugging Face hosts more than 2M models. This growing pool provides a rich base for model reuse and capability integration. Yet existing surveys often cover only separate parts of this space, and they do not provide a unified definition or a systematic taxonomy. This survey defines model fusion and organizes prior work into three levels: parameter-level, representation-level, and behavior-level fusion. We also review related metrics, benchmarks, and applications, summarize current challenges, and identify future directions. Our goal is to provide a clear map of this area and support future work on model fusion. A comprehensive list of papers about model fusion is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[MUSE: A Theory-Harnessed Story Engine for Vibe Narrativizing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15188)**  `arXiv:2609.15188`  `cs.CL`  
  _Jianxiang Ma, Xiaocui Yang, Daling Wang, Mingfu Zhang, Zijing Wang, Yuesong Hou, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLMs have been able to generate fluent prose, but high-quality stories also require coordinated decisions about plot, character, and language across planning, drafting, and revision. We formulate Vibe Narrativizing as turning natural-language writing requirements into a finished story. MUSE, a Theory-Harnessed Story Engine, addresses two bottlenecks: rule quality and sustained rule realization. Story theory supplies the rules, and a practical agent harness puts them to work. Knowledge engineering organizes Robert McKee's theory through rule atomization, semantic consolidation, mechanism abstraction, a single source of truth, and layered disclosure; typical examples clarify judgments that depend on context and aesthetic purpose. The harness preserves story decisions in intermediate deliverables across design, character performance, scene composition, and revision. Context engineering supplies each role with relevant guidance and decisions; a masterwork corpus provides inspiration and prose references. A worked example follows a requested object from its thematic role to climactic actions. Across four base models, MUSE improves WritingBench by 1.1 to 6.2 points over zero-shot generation; it is the only multi-stage system in our comparison to do so. It also raises LongStoryEval by more than ten points on three of the four models. ConStory-Bench consistency error density remains in the low single digits for all four models, below every reproduced story-system baseline on three of the four models. Ablations locate the largest quality contribution in structural design, voice-specific effects in the character path, and further gains in revision.
  </details>

- **[ModularRSI: Modular and Generalizable Recursive Harness Self-Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14857)**  `arXiv:2609.14857`  `cs.CL`  
  _Siwei Wu, Jincheng Ren, Yizhi Li, Haau-Sing Li, Chengran Yang, Xudong Ma, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent work extends recursive self-improvement (RSI) to agent harnesses for long-horizon coding and terminal tasks, enabling agents to improve execution mechanisms from experience. However, generalizable harness RSI remains challenging. First, evolving harnesses on evaluation benchmarks or their subsets makes it difficult to distinguish reusable improvements from benchmark-specific adaptation. Second, single-trajectory updates can conflate systematic harness deficiencies with instance-specific reasoning and solution details, producing modifications that transfer poorly to unseen tasks. Third, localizing recurring behavioral deficiencies within monolithic harnesses is difficult, while whole-harness optimization can entangle unrelated mechanisms and complicate attribution and validation. We propose ModularRSI, a benchmark-disjoint, contrastive, and modular framework for generalizable harness evolution. ModularRSI contrasts successful and failed trajectories for the same task and aggregates evidence across tasks to identify recurring behavioral deficiencies. It decomposes the evolvable harness into five functional modules: Agent Loop, Tool Use, Observation Management, Context Management, and Task Completion Detection. Each module evolves independently within a restricted modification scope, followed by an integration stage that combines the evolved modules into a unified harness and resolves potential conflicts. To support benchmark-disjoint evolution, we curate 2,000 executable evolution tasks from external sources that are disjoint from downstream evaluation benchmarks. Experiments on TB2.0 and SWE-Bench Verified show consistent improvements on unseen in-domain and cross-domain tasks, with the evolved harness also transferring across different foundation models.
  </details>

- **[LOOMSUM: Weaving Quantitative and Narrative Evidence for Faithful Long Text-Table Summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00241)**  `arXiv:2609.00241`  `cs.CL`  
  _Meng Zhou, Wenhao You, Wei Yuan, Yueying Tian_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long documents often distribute important information across extensive narrative passages and multiple tables, making faithful summarization particularly challenging. Existing methods may generate individually supported quantitative facts and analytical statements yet associate them incorrectly, producing quantitatively plausible yet analytically unfaithful summaries. In this work, we propose LOOMSUM, a training-free framework that extracts source-grounded atomic evidence, explicitly links table-derived facts with supporting narrative analyses, and plans the discourse structure before generation. We also introduce Table-Grounded Faithfulness (TGF), a claim-level metric that separately evaluates Numeric Grounding, Analysis Support, and Relation Consistency. Experiments on the text--table summarization benchmarks FINDSum and USTT show that LOOMSUM improves analytical faithfulness while maintaining strong summarization quality. Human evaluation finds positive component-level associations with the corresponding human judgments. Our Relation Consistency metric further shows stronger agreement with human relation judgments than generic factuality metrics, indicating that explicit cross-modal linking helps reduce errors in which supported quantities are paired with incorrect narrative interpretations. Together, these findings show that faithful long text--table summarization requires not only grounding individual facts, but also preserving the relations between them.
  </details>

- **[Every Token Leaves a Ripple in the Stream of Thought: Eliciting Model-Internal Token Saliency for Chain-of-Thought Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31066)**  `arXiv:2608.31066`  `cs.CL`  
  _Tianyi Zhao, Yinhan He, Wendy Zheng, Jundong Li, Chen Chen_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning improves multi-step problem solving, but long reasoning traces inflate inference cost. Token-level CoT compression reduces this cost by pruning full reasoning chains into shorter traces for model adaptation, making token selection the central challenge. Existing methods often rely on external scorers or heuristic signals only indirectly tied to the model's internal answer computation. We instead adopt a model-internal perspective: as the model forms an answer, each reasoning token induces a ripple in the residual stream whose effect on the answer reflects the token's contribution to the underlying computation. Building on this view, we propose \textsc{MIST} (Model-Internal Saliency for Token-level CoT compression), which defines token importance along two complementary axes: \emph{necessity}, the drop in answer likelihood when a token's internal contribution is removed, and \emph{sufficiency}, the gain in answer likelihood when that contribution alone is provided. Combining the two yields a unified importance score for pruning.
