- **[Trajectory-Refined Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08432)**  `arXiv:2606.08432`  `cs.AI`  
  _Li Jiang, Haoran Xu, Yichuan Ding, Amy Zhang_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a central post-training tool for large language models (LLMs), providing dense per-token teacher supervision along the student's own rollouts. In this work, we identify a common structural cause underlying OPD, which we call prefix failure. Under prefix failure, dense per-token supervision induces a bimodal teacher mixture and fragmented gradients that token-level loss truncation or reweighting fail to address. We thus propose Trajectory-Refined Distillation (TRD), a trajectory-level correction method that revises the student's rollout under the teacher guidance while within on-policy support. By correcting problematic prefixes before distillation, TRD mitigates prefix failure at its source. Moreover, TRD improves exploration by exposing the student to alternative valid derivations under teacher guidance, even when the original rollouts are already correct. TRD can also be applied to on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), a parameter-sharing variant that uses the student model conditioned on privileged information as the teacher. TRD improves average math accuracy while remaining competitive on code. Under OPSD, it solves $9/23$ AMOBench questions left unsolved by the Qwen3-8B base model, nearly doubling the strongest dense-KL baseline. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Planning Takes More Than Token Prediction: Causal Plan for Benchmarking and Building Physically Grounded Embodied Reasoners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01810)**  `arXiv:2606.01810`  `cs.AI`  
  _Zirui Song, Zheng Lu, Mingqi Gao, Qinlei Xie, Wanqi Zhong, Hanwen Cui, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Current benchmarks for embodied vision-language planning inadvertently favor linguistic next-token prediction over physically grounded next-state reasoning. This rewards models that mimic statistical language priors rather than track true causal dependencies, reducing complex physical planning to shallow sequence modeling. Hence, achieving genuine physical autonomy requires a fundamental shift from linguistically grounded token prediction toward physically grounded causal reasoning. To this end, we introduce Causal-Plan-Bench, a high-fidelity diagnostic suite spanning four causal dimensions, curated via multi-stage verification. To endow models with this capability, a four-stage annotation pipeline extracts structured interaction records from egocentric videos to construct Causal-Plan-1M, a dense million-scale corpus of explicit causal reasoning traces. Extensive evaluation reveals a striking gap: leading models struggle to demonstrate genuine physical agency -- even GPT-6-astra scores only 43.04. In contrast, our tailored training recipe enables Causal Planner to internalize the complex physical logic required for accurate next-state estimation. Built upon Qwen3-VL-8B, Causal Planner raises its backbone's score from 33.23 to 45.28, a 36.3% relative gain, and improves on three external benchmarks without benchmark-specific adaptation. We further observe an empirical Causal-Supervision Scaling Trend. Paired no-vision controls also reveal substantial visual dependence, while cross-judge comparisons and human scoring assess the reliability of automated evaluation. More importantly, we initiate the first effort to turn agents from superficial token predictors into physically grounded causal reasoners, bridging language modeling and world modeling.
  </details>

- **[CoMIC: Collaborative Memory and Insights Circulation for Long-Horizon LLM Agents in Web Cloud-Edge Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00756)**  `arXiv:2606.00756`  `cs.AI`  
  _Yannan Wang, Longli Yang, Zhen Liu, Abhishek Kumar, Carsten Maple_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM-based Web agents are increasingly deployed on edge servers to carry out long-horizon tasks on behalf of users with low latency. However, the lightweight models that fit on edge servers often struggle with long-horizon tasks that require persistent memory, subgoal tracking, and reflection. Fine-tuning edge models after deployment is costly and difficult to scale across heterogeneous nodes, while purely local execution confines each agent to its own isolated experience. We propose \textsc{CoMIC}, a parameter-update-free cloud-edge framework for Collaborative Memory and Insights Circulation. Following the paradigm of ``Act at the Edge, Reflect in the Cloud'', edge agents execute locally with subgoal-oriented hierarchical memory and selective re-expansion of relevant histories, while a cloud-side LLM critic asynchronously evaluates the trajectories uploaded through a Web gateway, admits reusable experience, and circulates cross-agent guidance indexed by semantic subgoal identifiers back to all edge agents. On five long-horizon benchmarks, \textsc{CoMIC} enables weak edge agents to achieve non-zero success on tasks where a standard memory-based agent fails entirely, and improves their task progress over both the standard agent and purely local execution while reducing context consumption relative to the standard agent, all without updating model parameters. When stronger heterogeneous agents join the edge, the weak agents further improve in success, progress, and grounding with lower context consumption.
  </details>

- **[ConMoE: MoE Compression as Expert Selection and Functional Assignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29350)**  `arXiv:2605.29350`  `cs.AI`  
  _Yilun Yao, Jiaming Pan, Elsie Dai, Peizhuang Cong, Chao-Hsuan Liu, Yaoming Li, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity through sparse activation, but storing their full parameters remains costly in GPU memory. Existing expert compression methods address this problem through pruning, merging, or substitution, typically coupling expert pool construction with the assignment of routed workloads. In this work, we formulate expert compression as two decisions--constructing an expert pool and assigning the original experts' workloads to that pool--and show that assignment can be optimized after the pool is fixed. Based on this formulation, we introduce ConMoE, which constructs a compact pool using Anchor Coverage and optimizes assignment through a router-conditioned functional objective derived from a layer reconstruction bound, treating parameter proximity only as a proxy. ConMoE uses unlabeled calibration inputs and keeps the router and expert weights frozen. With the pool fixed, functional assignment improves macro accuracy by 1.82 and 0.35 percentage points at 50% and 75% expert retention, respectively, and also improves pools constructed by other selectors. With task-specific calibration across three MoE architectures and six zero-shot benchmarks, ConMoE achieves the highest macro average among the compared methods at both ratios. At 50% expert retention, ConMoE reduces peak GPU memory by 29.6-48.4% relative to the uncompressed models on our generation workloads. These results establish expert assignment as an independent optimization axis for MoE compression.
  </details>

- **[TADDLE: A Tool-Augmented Agent for Detecting Deficient LLM-Generated Peer Reviews](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26911)**  `arXiv:2605.26911`  `cs.AI`  
  _Hanqi Duan, Xiang Li_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM-generated peer reviews are increasingly common at major venues, yet their deficiencies are hard to detect because they are uniformly fluent and well-structured. Existing work either classifies authorship without judging quality, or scores quality with features designed for human-written reviews; no prior system detects deficiencies in LLM-generated reviews at the level of individual defect types. To bridge the gap, we introduce TADDLE, a Tool-Augmented Agent for Detecting Deficient LLM-Generated Peer Reviews, together with the first expert-annotated benchmark for this task. Our benchmark comprises 1,800 reviews on 50 ICLR 2025 papers, multi-label-annotated by 18 domain experts against a taxonomy of six defect categories (plus a non-deficient label). TADDLE decomposes detection into four specialized analysis tools -- Verify, Correct, Complete, and Transform -- orchestrated by an agent; an integrator synthesizes their outputs into binary and multi-label classifications via two-stage semi-supervised learning. Experiments show that TADDLE performs strongly on binary detection and the multi-label classification task. We release the benchmark and code atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Verifiable Process Rewards for Agentic Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10325)**  `arXiv:2605.10325`  `cs.AI`  
  _Huining Yuan, Zelai Xu, Huaijie Wang, Xiangmin Yi, Jiaxuan Gao, Xiao-Ping Zhang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) has improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet existing approaches predominantly rely on sparse outcome-level feedback, posing a substantial credit-assignment challenge in long-horizon agentic tasks. In this work, we study structured agentic reasoning problems that admit symbolic or algorithmic task-solving oracles. We propose Verifiable Process Rewards (VPR), a training framework that repurposes such task oracles as action-level process verifiers, providing dense rewards for intermediate actions and enabling fine-grained credit assignment. We instantiate VPR in three distinct settings: a search-based oracle for Sokoban, a constraint-based oracle for Sudoku, and a posterior-based oracle for Minesweeper. To optimize policies with these rewards, we introduce oracle-guided state-group rollout and locally normalized optimization. Empirically, VPR-trained Qwen3-4B outperforms outcome-reward GRPO and VinePPO across all three training environments. When jointly trained on math data and all three game environments, VPR achieves the highest average general-reasoning performance and strongest agentic results among the compared training configurations. To further assess its applicability to more general agentic tool-use settings, we apply VPR-style action-level supervision to $\tau^2$-bench using an expert LLM as a reference policy and observe improved performance over outcome-reward GRPO on held-out tasks. Together, these results position VPR as a promising approach for leveraging reliable task oracles to improve agentic reasoning, while highlighting its dependence on the availability and reliability of task oracles and the challenge of extending intermediate verification to less structured, open-ended environments.
  </details>

- **[MemQ: Integrating Q-Learning into Self-Evolving Memory Agents over Provenance DAGs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08374)**  `arXiv:2605.08374`  `cs.AI`  
  _Junwei Liao, Haoting Shi, Ruiwen Zhou, Jiaqian Wang, Shengtao Zhang, Wei Zhang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Episodic memory allows LLM agents to accumulate and retrieve experience, but current methods treat each memory independently, i.e., evaluating retrieval quality in isolation without accounting for the dependency chains through which memories enable the creation of future memories. We introduce MemQ, which applies TD($\lambda$) eligibility traces to memory Q-values, propagating credit backward through a provenance DAG that records which memories were retrieved when each new memory was created. Credit weight decays as $(\gamma\lambda)^d$ with DAG depth $d$, replacing temporal distance with structural proximity. We formalize this setting as an Exogenous-Context MDP, separating externally supplied tasks from the evolving memory store, and represent retrieval-set values by a first-order mean of per-memory values plus an explicit approximation residual. Across five interaction, code-generation, and agentic benchmarks, MemQ improves average held-out, final runtime, and cumulative success rates over the baseline with the highest average for each metric by 2.53, 4.23, and 2.13 percentage points, respectively. Ablations on LiveCodeBench, BFCL, and DSBench support the benefit of bootstrapping and multi-depth credit propagation. Analyses of Q-values and runtime learning show that learned memory values are associated with subsequent success and that MemQ retains more of its historical task coverage. We also explore the limits of MemQ's benefits using multiple-choice reasoning tasks, where limited interaction offers fewer opportunities to reuse procedural experience. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Tools as Continuous Flow for Evolving Agentic Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07339)**  `arXiv:2605.07339`  `cs.AI`  
  _Tairan Huang, Siyu Shang, Qiang Chen, Xiu Su, Yi Chen_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in orchestrating tools for reasoning tasks. However, existing methods rely on a step-wise paradigm that lacks a global perspective, which causes error accumulation over long horizons and restricts generalization to unseen tools. To overcome these limitations, we propose Tools as Continuous Flow for Evolving Agentic Reasoning (FlowAgent), which reconceptualizes tool chaining as continuous trajectory generation within a semantic space. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we introduce the first plan-level closed-loop benchmark dedicated to plan-level agentic reasoning in dynamic real-world environments. Specifically, the proposed FlowAgent leverages conditional flow matching to generate continuous latent trajectories, providing a global planning perspective to ensure coherent and robust tool execution. Theoretically, we establish formal bounds on utility convergence and prove that our continuous formulation fundamentally guarantees robust generalization and error attenuation. Empirical evaluations show that FlowAgent achieves superior robustness and adaptability in long-horizon reasoning tasks.
  </details>

- **[OracleProto: A Reproducible Framework for Benchmarking LLM Forecasting via Knowledge Cutoffs and Temporal Masking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03762)**  `arXiv:2605.03762`  `cs.AI`  
  _Yiding Ma, Chengyun Ruan, Kaibo Huang, Jin Tan, Zhongliang Yang, Linna Zhou_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Forecasting is a composite capability encompassing information gathering, evidence integration, situational assessment, and decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) combine reasoning and tool use, offering new avenues for automated forecasting and decision support. Yet LLM forecasting evaluation faces a structural challenge: live benchmarks support prospective assessment, but limited question reuse and changing information conditions make results difficult to reproduce and compare; retrospective benchmarks offer reproducibility but risk information leakage. We introduce OracleProto, a reproducible framework for evaluating LLM forecasting in a controlled, temporally masked environment. Through model knowledge cutoff constraints and temporal masking, OracleProto constructs a temporal sandbox for real-world web retrieval, audits information boundaries through leakage detection, and reconstructs resolved events as forecasting instances. Discrete answer normalization and hierarchical scoring enable unified evaluation. We evaluate 27 model-configuration pairs on 300 FutureX-Past-derived questions over 24,300 prediction trials, assessing forecasting quality, sampling stability, and cost efficiency under controlled information boundaries. An audit finds only 1.37% residual leakage in retrieval results after temporal masking and leakage filtering. OracleProto retains resolved forecasting tasks as reusable evaluation resources under explicit temporal boundaries, supporting continual accumulation of forecasting datasets and systematic evaluation of forecasting capabilities. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[ScoringBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Tabular Foundation Models with Proper Scoring Rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29928)**  `arXiv:2603.29928`  `cs.AI`  
  _Jonas Landsgesell, Pascal Knoll, Tizian Wenzel_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN, TabICL, ExaOneTabular, and Nori already produce full predictive distributions, yet prevailing regression benchmarks evaluate them almost exclusively via point-estimate metrics such as RMSE. This overlooks the distributional information these models are designed to provide. We introduce ScoringBench, an open and extensible benchmark that evaluates tabular regression models under a comprehensive suite of proper scoring rules - including (weighted) CRPS, energy scores and interval scores - alongside standard point metrics. ScoringBench covers 101 regression datasets from diverse domains, supports transparent community contributions via a git-based leaderboard, and provides two complementary ranking protocols: an ordinal Demsar/autorank approach and a magnitude-preserving $z$-score ranking approach. Our evaluation of various model types, including (fine-tuned) tabular foundation models, gradient-boosted trees, and MLPs, shows that model rankings shift depending on the chosen scoring rule. Models that perform well on point-estimate metrics can rank lower on probabilistic ones. These findings demonstrate that evaluation metric selection is a core modeling decision and a domain-specific requirement for applications where certain types of errors carry higher consequences.
  </details>

- **[The Token Games: Evaluating Language Model Reasoning with Puzzle Duels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17831)**  `arXiv:2602.17831`  `cs.AI`  
  _Simon Henniger, Gabriel Poesia_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Evaluating the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models is increasingly challenging as models improve. Human curation of hard questions is highly expensive, especially in recent benchmarks using PhD-level domain knowledge to challenge the most capable models. Even then, there is always a concern about whether these questions test genuine reasoning or if similar problems have been seen during training. Here, we take inspiration from 16th-century mathematical duels to design The Token Games (TTG): an evaluation framework where models challenge each other by creating their own puzzles. We leverage the format of Programming Puzzles - given a function that returns a boolean, find inputs that make it return True - to flexibly represent problems and enable verifying solutions. Using results from pairwise duels, we then compute Elo ratings, allowing us to compare models relative to each other. We evaluate 10 frontier models on TTG, and closely match the ranking from existing benchmarks such as Humanity's Last Exam, spending less than $200 USD and without involving any human effort in creating puzzles. We also find that creating good puzzles is still a highly challenging task for current models. Overall, our work suggests new paradigms for evaluating reasoning that avoid saturation by design, and that allow testing models for other skills like creativity and task creation alongside problem solving.
  </details>

- **[Risky-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Safety Risks in Real-World Life-Assist Deployments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03100)**  `arXiv:2602.03100`  `cs.AI`  
  _Jingnan Zheng, Yanzhen Luo, Jingjun Xu, Bingnan Liu, Yuxin Chen, Chenhang Cui, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that operate in real-world environments, introducing safety risks beyond linguistic harm through tool use, external transactions, and multi-step decision making. Existing agent safety evaluations construct risk-oriented tasks that lack a hierarchically organized taxonomy of attack surfaces, rely on predefined harm categories rather than deployment-grounded safety rubrics, and evaluate agent behavior in isolation rather than during realistic, long-horizon task execution. To address these limitations, we propose Risky-Bench, a deployment-grounded framework for systematic agent safety evaluation in life-assist settings. Risky-Bench derives context-aware safety rubrics from domain-agnostic safety principles and systematically probes safety risks across hierarchically organized attack surfaces through realistic task execution under varying threat assumptions. Applied to life-assist scenarios covering food delivery, in-store assistance, and online travel booking, Risky-Bench evaluates seven state-of-the-art agents across 750 tasks, revealing attack success rates ranging from 25% to 60% and exposing systematic failure patterns including threat-model-specific vulnerabilities, attack-surface-dependent risk concentration, and model-dependent effects of explicit reasoning. Our code and data are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[GDEPO: Group Dual-dynamic and Equal-right Advantage Policy Optimization for Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06795)**  `arXiv:2601.06795`  `cs.AI`  
  _Zhengqing Yan, Fan Guo, Xinyang Liu, Yi Zhang, Yao Liu, Qi Liu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Automated Theorem Proving (ATP) is a fundamental AI challenge, requiring machine-verifiable proofs in formal languages like Lean to evaluate reasoning. Reinforcement Learning (RL), especially Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is a mainstream approach. However, GRPO faces two critical issues in ATP: its relative advantage estimation may conflict with binary verifier feedback under composite rewards, and its static sampling strategy discards batches without valid proofs, causing data waste. Repeated training on mastered problems also wastes computation. To address this, we propose Group Dual-dynamic and Equal-right Advantage Policy Optimization (GDEPO), incorporating three core mechanisms: 1) dynamic additional sampling, resampling ineffective batches until a valid proof is found; 2) equal-right advantage, decoupling the advantage function's sign (correctness) from its magnitude (auxiliary rewards) to ensure stable policy updates while increasing effective computation; and 3) dynamic additional iterations, applying extra gradient steps to initially failed but eventually successful samples to accelerate learning. Experiments on MinF2F-test, MathOlympiadBench, and PutnamBench confirm GDEPO's effectiveness, with ablation studies validating its synergistic components. The method enhances data utilization and optimization efficiency, offering a novel training paradigm for ATP.
  </details>

- **[Decomposability-Guided Cooperative Coevolution for Large-Scale Itinerary Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06121)**  `arXiv:2506.06121`  `cs.AI`  
  _Ziyu Zhang, Peilan Xu, Yuetong Sun, Yuhui Shi, Wenjian Luo_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large-scale itinerary planning is a variant of the traveling salesman problem, aiming to determine an optimal path that maximizes the collected point-of-interest (POI) scores while minimizing travel time and cost, subject to travel duration constraints. This paper analyzes inter-component dependence in large-scale itinerary planning and establishes sufficient conditions for weak decomposability, under which an optimal path can visit each cluster as a contiguous subpath. Guided by this weak decomposability, we propose a novel multi-objective cooperative coevolutionary algorithm for large-scale itinerary planning, addressing the challenges of component imbalance and interactions. Specifically, we design a dynamic decomposition strategy based on the normalized fitness within each component, define optimization potential considering component scale and contribution, and develop a computational resource allocation strategy. Finally, we evaluate the proposed algorithm on 18 real-world test cases, eight large-scale semi-synthetic test cases, and eight adapted public clustered orienteering problem benchmark cases. Comparative results show that the proposed algorithm achieves the highest mean hypervolume across all 34 test cases and significantly outperforms the compared algorithms. Ablation and optimizer-decoupling analyses further validate the effectiveness of its core mechanisms and the general applicability of the proposed framework, with particularly pronounced performance gains on large-scale benchmark instances.
  </details>

- **[Physics: Benchmarking Foundation Models on University-Level Physics Problem Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.21821)**  `arXiv:2503.21821`  `cs.AI`  
  _Kaiyue Feng, Yilun Zhao, Yixin Liu, Tianyu Yang, Chen Zhao, John Sous, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce Physics, a benchmark for evaluating foundation models on advanced physics problem solving. It contains 1034 annotated, open-ended problems from PhD-qualifying exams across six core physics domains. Solving these problems requires applying domain-specific knowledge to physical setups and carrying out multi-step mathematical reasoning. Each problem includes a worked solution and independently checked reference answers. An LLM-based grading protocol evaluates individual answers and complete multi-part problems, supporting numeric, symbolic, and text responses. We evaluate 53 proprietary and open-weight models. On test problems without figures, high accuracy is concentrated in a small group of thinking models, with the strongest open-weight models approaching proprietary performance. Most open-weight models still solve fewer than half of these problems. Our analysis of Qwen3.5-9B reveals failures in applying physics knowledge and interpreting figures, with misread figures affecting several subquestions.
  </details>
